Summary

Three through stations under Paris

Every long-distance train to Paris ends in a dead-end station. This study tests replacing the four terminals used by high-speed trains by three deep through stations, Paris Nord-Est, Gare de Lyon and Montparnasse, joined by two pairs of tunnels and a direct link between the two southern stations, so that high-speed, regional and suburban trains run across the city. No train reverses, every station has direct trains to every direction, and nobody is further from a train than today. It would cost about €40 billion (€27 to 60 billion across unit prices and risk), and on the benefits that can be counted so far it does not pay for itself.

€40bnto build, with 15% for risk€27 to 60bn across the range of unit prices and of risk
27.4 → 22.8minfrom a point in Paris to a station where the train stopsNo point is further than today. 24.5 min if the train's ride between its Paris stops is counted and the passenger picks a train that calls at their best station
190%of running costs coveredWith track charges on new TGV journeys, charges on new uses of the TGV and on regional express passengers, and half of the operators' saving on trainsets. 165% to 269% across the range of running costs; 165% with the charge on high-speed passengers alone
70%of the yearly cost returned in benefits99% with 1.5% yearly growth. Comparable tunnels were approved at 0.5 to 2 times their cost on their own basis, about 0.8 to 1.2 for the Elizabeth line on ours

The findings

Passengers

Reaching a train gets quicker everywhere in Paris. Every station has direct trains to every direction, so the average time to a station where your train stops falls from 27.4 to 22.8 minutes at the door, 24.5 once the train's ride between its Paris stops is counted. The stations stay where they are: no point loses.

Crossing Paris

5.2 million passengers a year stop changing stations by metro. A change that takes 57.5 minutes today becomes a direct train or a change of platform: Atlantic to south-east in 6 minutes by the link, no reversal. Regional trains run on to a second station.

Cost

€40.5 billion, with 15% for risk on top of unit prices that already hold past overruns, because no station has been designed. Stations, €13.9 billion, and tunnels, €8.5 billion, are the two largest items of the €27.7 billion of works.

Traffic

+13.6 million high-speed and +23.7 million regional journeys a year. Most of the high-speed gain is between cities on two lines, which today need two or three changes in Paris: their traffic grows 3.1 times. The charge falls only on new uses, so no journey is lost. Passengers who go round Paris or avoid the train, and traffic growth, are not yet sized: they are study points.

Financing

Operations pay for themselves; construction cannot be repaid. Track charges on the new journeys, charges on new uses of the TGV and on regional express passengers, and half of the trainset saving cover 190% of running costs, and the surplus goes to construction. No land is sold. Construction needs a grant of €11 billion, 26% of the cost, on top of a business tax package: public money in all is about 80% of the cost.

Economic return

Benefits counted: €1,505 million a year, 70% of the yearly cost, 99% with growth. Public budgets get back about €442 million a year in taxes. The four parks on the terminal sites are not valued yet, nor is room for more trains.

The two accounts at a glance

What this means

As counted here, operations pay for themselves with a surplus, but construction is a public investment paid by taxes and grants for 80% of its cost: a grant of €11 billion on top of a new tax on businesses. Counted benefits return 70% of the yearly cost, at the low end of comparable tunnels. That is not yet a case for building, and not a case against studying: the count leaves out the reason most cities gave for through stations, capacity for more trains; the regional network run as through lines; the province to province market that would cross Paris without a change; and the four parks on the terminal sites. It rests on prices and running costs taken from few records.

Five investigations would move the answer most: what limits the number of trains today; a fresh count of the passengers who cross Paris; the running costs net of what today's terminals cost; the region's travel model, for the regional lines; and the value of the parks. They are listed in what to verify.

How to use this document

The chapters follow the argument: the problem, what would be built, how it would run, what passengers gain, what it costs, who pays, what the country gets back, what could change the answer. Each can be read alone. Blue links with an arrow jump to the place where a point is treated; small numbers open the source.

Most figures can be explored: move a price in the cost chapter, a charge or a tax in the financing calculator, tap a point on the access map, pair two lines in crossing Paris, step through the works in the timeline.

Words used throughout. TGV: the French high-speed train. RER: the express suburban lines that already cross Paris underground. The link: the direct tunnel between the city ends of Montparnasse and Gare de Lyon, about 5 km assumption, which lets a train from the Atlantic run on to the south-east without passing through Nord-Est.

Three annexes explain the precedents the project draws on: how Zürich turned a terminus into a through station under a working hall, what the Elizabeth line changed in London and how it was paid for, and how the Swiss timetable makes every train meet every train.

Every number comes from a small model described in method and assumptions, or from a document listed in the sources. Assumptions are marked assumption, drawings that are not designs illustrative sketch. No station has been designed; this is a first test of whether the idea is worth a study.

Chapter 1

Why Paris stops every train

Every long-distance line into Paris ends at a buffer stop, in one of four separate stations. So every train has to turn round, a passenger crossing France has to cross the city by metro, and the busiest stations are short of room for more trains. Other cities have removed the same problem by running trains through.

Four stations, four dead ends

4terminals for high-speed trainsGare du Nord, Gare de l'Est, Gare de Lyon and Montparnasse. Inside Paris, no track joins one to another for long-distance trains
118platform tracks in the fourRER platforms included. Derived from published track lists, partly unverified1
5.2millionpassengers a year change station in ParisDerived from the last survey, in 2012-13, which counted 13,000 a day in the region2
57.5minfrom train to trainTaken in this study for a change of station today assumption The range assumed is 45 to 70 minutes

High-speed trains (TGV) from the north arrive at Gare du Nord, from the east at Gare de l'Est, from the south-east at Gare de Lyon and from the Atlantic coast at Montparnasse. Suburban and regional trains end at the same four stations.

All four are terminals: the track stops at the end of the platform, and a train can only leave the way it came. A through station is the opposite: trains arrive at one end and leave by the other, without turning back.

Three things follow from the dead ends. A train holds its platform for a long time while it turns round. A traveller whose trip continues beyond Paris has to change station. And each line reaches only one corner of the city. The rest of this chapter takes them in turn.

Words used in this report
  • TGV: the French high-speed train. A full train is 400 m long; two coupled sets carry more than 1,000 passengers.
  • RER: the five express lines, A to E, that already cross Paris underground. Suburban lines H, K, P, N and R do not: they end at the terminals.
  • Regional express: trains from towns 50 to 250 km away (TER and Intercités), which also end at the terminals.
  • Hall: the large room of a station where passengers wait before going to the platforms.

A terminal uses its platforms badly, and the big ones are short of room

A train that arrives at a terminal is emptied, checked, often cleaned and restocked, filled again, and sent back out across the tracks it came in on. At Montparnasse the nine tracks kept for high-speed trains give at most nine departures an hour: one train per track per hour.4 A TGV that only stops needs 3 minutes, or 4 to 5 at the largest stations.5 Through stations are planned for four to six long-distance trains an hour on each platform track: Stuttgart's new station, not yet open, reached about six in a simulated stress test.6 7 One that is in service, Zürich's Löwenstrasse station, handles about 460 trains a day on four tracks, about six an hour on each on average,8 though the through trains that wait for connections there stand 6 to 9 minutes (derived from the departure boards; see Zürich).9 10

The rule this study uses for its own stations. Platforms are dedicated by direction, 3 tracks each way at each station. A stop takes 4 minutes; after a departure the track needs about 3 minutes before the next train can arrive; and a timetable can use about 65% of that 7-minute cycle and still absorb late trains. So one track takes about 5.6 trains an hour assumption, all three figures. Two tracks each way would do on paper; the third takes the late trains. What limits the number of trains today, the platforms or the lines outside Paris, is a study point (I1 in what to verify). How the rule sizes the new stations is in how many platforms.

  • Gare du Nord was turned down as the terminal of the airport express for lack of capacity.13 It already handles 2,200 trains and 700,000 passengers a day.14
  • Gare de Lyon must find room. The high-speed line to Lyon is being upgraded from 13 to 16 trains an hour each way by 2030, and the station has to take them.15
  • The tracks cut the city. Approach tracks and platforms run from each terminal out to the ring road and divide the neighbourhoods on both sides. What the project would free is in changes to today's stations.

Crossing France means crossing Paris by metro

A traveller from Lille to Lyon gets off at Gare du Nord, takes the RER or the metro to Gare de Lyon and boards a second train. The last survey, in 2012-13, counted 13,000 passengers a day changing between two stations in the region.2 Scaled by the growth of high-speed traffic since, that is about 5.2 million a year (derived; no newer count is published). With the stations joined, the same traveller stays on the train, or changes on the platforms of one station.

Some trains already go round Paris. The bypass line east of the city, opened in 1994 to 1996, carries trains from one region to another without entering Paris, with stops at Marne-la-Vallée, Roissy and Massy. They carried 21.9 million passengers in 2009, 17.6 million of them on trains through those outer stations.16 For the pairs that include the Atlantic line they are slow and few: Bordeaux to Lille takes 4h47 on the direct train round Paris and 4h21 with a change of station in Paris,17 against about 3h25 through Paris by this study's arithmetic (2h04 Bordeaux to Paris and 1h02 Paris to Lille on the best trains, about 20 minutes across the city; to verify) assumption. The passengers these trains do not carry, by car, by air or not travelling, are not in the count above; crossing Paris by TGV comes back to them.

The seats are short where the gain is largest. On the Atlantic line a new operator, Velvet, has ordered 12 trains to run between Paris and Bordeaux, Nantes, Rennes and Angers from 2028, and says it will add 10 million seats a year to a market where, by its own account, 15% of would-be rail passengers go by car, coach or air for want of trains.18 The line to Lyon is being upgraded from 13 to 16 trains an hour each way by 2030.15 Demand is there; the terminals are where it meets its limit.

Two other groups of passengers pay for the dead ends.

  • Each traveller has one station to go to. A Parisian leaving for Bordeaux must reach Montparnasse, wherever in the city the trip starts. From the north-east of Paris that is a long metro ride with changes. Reaching the station measures it.
  • Suburban lines stop at the edge of the centre. Lines H, K, P, N and R each end at a terminal. A commuter from the northern suburbs who works in the south of Paris changes to the metro at Gare du Nord. Regional and suburban passengers gives the numbers.
Other cities have done it

Zürich put four through tracks under its terminal, Vienna replaced two terminals with one through station, and Stuttgart is replacing 16 terminal platforms with 8 through tracks.8 19 6 Paris itself did it for part of its suburban network with the RER. The annexes on Zürich and London give the record of two of them, and the next chapter describes what would be built in Paris.

Chapter 2

What would be built

Three deep stations under the existing ones, joined by 26.8 km of tunnel routes, with nothing left on the surface but the station halls. Every train stops at two of the three stations, and every station has direct trains to all four directions, on half of the trains of each line. Nothing here has been designed: the map and the quantities are planning assumptions.

Three stations and seven tunnel corridors

3deep through stationsParis Nord-Est, Gare de Lyon and Montparnasse: 40 platform tracks, 16, 12 and 12
26.8kmof route in seven corridors49 km of twin-track tunnel: two pairs of tracks on 21.8 km, one pair on the 5 km link between Montparnasse and Gare de Lyon
13.9kmof platform track400 m long for TGVs, 350 m for regional express trains, 225 m for suburban trains
4station halls kept, parks in place of the tracksThe listed halls of Gare du Nord, Gare de l’Est and Gare de Lyon, and the recent hall of Montparnasse, become the entrances to the stations below. The surface tracks become parks

A through station is a station where trains arrive at one end and leave by the other, without turning back. A corridor is a route followed by two tunnels side by side, each with two tracks; the link has one tunnel. A portal is the place where a tunnel comes up to join an existing line. An underground junction is a cavern where two tunnels become one. The TGV is the French high-speed train. Regional express trains are the TER services that join Paris to the towns of the surrounding regions. The RER is the set of express suburban lines that cross Paris underground.

The corridors run from each station to the existing tracks at the ring road, where the tunnels come up; on the eastern line they come up at Rosa Parks, just inside it. A tunnel 35 to 40 m deep needs only about 1.1 to 1.2 km to reach the surface, and a kilometre kept underground costs far more than a kilometre of existing track, so the tunnels go no further. The three stations form a triangle: two sides of it are the corridors through Paris Nord-Est, the third is the direct link between the two southern stations. Switch layers on and off, and select a station, a corridor, a portal or a junction to read its facts.

Two networks in the tunnels

Each corridor carries two pairs of tracks, each pair in a tunnel of its own. One pair is for the main-line trains, TGVs and regional express trains together, as on the surface today. The other is for the suburban trains: lines H and K from the north run on to line N in the Atlantic, and line P from the east on to line R in the south-east. The link between Montparnasse and Gare de Lyon is one pair of tracks for TGVs only.

One corridor, seen in cross-section

Cross-section of one corridor, not to scale illustrative sketch. On the RER E extension opened in 2024, one tunnel 9.6 m wide inside carries two tracks.20

Why two, and not one or three

  • Suburban trains apart. They stop more often and run to a tighter rhythm. On their own pair, a late suburban train never holds up a TGV, and the pair can be signalled like a metro line.
  • TGVs and regional express trains together, as in Zürich, Vienna and Stuttgart.8 19 6 In the stations each kind has platforms of its own, so the two share only the running tunnels.
  • The link for TGVs only. It exists for the 9 trains an hour each way between the Atlantic and the south-east when both lines are full; no regional or suburban train needs it.
  • What it adds up to. 21.8 km of route with two tunnels and 5 km with one: 49 km of two-track tunnel, 8 portals and 6 junction caverns.

Whether one suburban pair takes the whole peak of lines H, K and P is a study point: a third pair of tunnels on the two sides of the triangle would cost about €7 billion more (derived from the unit prices). The cost is built up in the cost chapter; which trains use which tracks, and how the link is used, is in trains and timetable.

Left as it is

  • The five RER lines, A to E, which already cross Paris underground.
  • The metro.
  • Saint-Lazare, Austerlitz and Bercy stations.
  • The train depots, which stay beside the approach lines; see changes at today's stations.

Not included in the cost

  • New trains.
  • Clearing the surface tracks once they are closed, and making the parks.
  • Anything built beside the parks.

How the stations sit under the present ones is in the three stations. How all this could be built while trains keep running is in works and stages.

Four parks where the tracks were

No surface platform is kept for trains. Once the deep stations are open, the four fans of tracks inside Paris are no longer needed: the two fans north of Gare du Nord and Gare de l’Est, the tracks from Gare de Lyon towards Bercy, and the tracks from Montparnasse to the ring road. The project turns them into four park areas. About 160 hectares could be released in all, an estimate read from maps assumption; no official measure of the four track corridors exists. The one published figure found is about 30 hectares of rail corridor inside the Bercy-Charenton development area (derived).24

What stays

  • The four halls, as entrances to the stations below.
  • The RER and metro stations under them.
  • The depots, beyond the ring road, reached through the portals and the existing tracks.

What is not counted

  • The land is not sold: no income from it enters the accounts.
  • The parks are not valued: no benefit from them enters the economic return.
  • Clearing the tracks and making the parks are not in the cost. Their area, value and cost are a study point.

Two points are open. The airport express train to Roissy is due to end at surface platforms of Gare de l’Est;13 what becomes of it has not been studied. And whether Gare du Nord can be emptied at the peak depends on one suburban pair carrying the whole peak of lines H, K and P, which has not been checked against a timetable; see two networks in the tunnels.

Chapter 3

How the stations would be laid out

Nobody has designed these stations. This chapter sketches where each would sit under the present station, what is already underground there, and how a passenger would get from the street down to the train. In the illustration used by the model, reaching a deep platform takes 4.0 minutes from the hall, against 3.7 minutes to walk down a terminal platform today. That near-equality rests on assumptions that a concept design must check.

Paris Nord-Est: one station under two halls

How to read the drawings

Every drawing in this chapter is an illustrative sketch. Only dimensions with a source, or taken from the model, are printed as numbers. Positions, shapes and the order of the platforms are invented to make the sketch readable. Dashed outlines mark structures whose depth is not published.

Gare du Nord and Gare de l’Est are 500 m apart; the walk between them takes 8 to 14 minutes today.3 Between the two, about 30 m down, lies Magenta, a station opened in 1999 on line E of the RER, the express suburban lines that cross Paris underground: 4 tracks in a cavern 225 m long and 54 m wide.23

The new station would be entered from either hall. It has 16 platform tracks: 6 for TGVs at 400 m, grouped three for trains towards the north and the east and three for trains towards the south, 6 for regional express trains at 350 m, and 4 for suburban trains at 225 m. That is about 6 times the platform length of Magenta. Nothing of this size has been built under Paris. The deep through stations of Stuttgart and Berlin have 8 tracks each (Berlin unverified).6 25

What is not known. Whether 16 tracks fit on one level between the two halls, at what depth, and how they pass Magenta, the RER station of Gare du Nord and three metro lines. This station alone is carried at €7.9 billion with design, land and 15% risk, 19% of the whole project. A concept design of it is the first study to commission; see what to verify.

Gare de Lyon: beside a five-level RER station, near the Seine

Gare de Lyon has 22 surface tracks in two halls (unverified);31 the seven platforms of Hall 1 are already 400 m long.32 Its underground station is one of the largest in Paris: RER lines A and D on five levels, 315 m long and 41 m wide, with RER D above RER A (unverified).33 The RER D tunnel is 20 m deep.34 Metro line 14 runs beside it (unverified).35

The new station would have 12 platform tracks: 6 for TGVs, three each way, 4 for regional express trains and 2 for suburban trains. At its city end the TGV tracks fork: towards Paris Nord-Est, and towards the direct link to Montparnasse, 5 km long, which passes under the Seine. The natural place for the station is under today's surface platforms, beside the RER station. Neither the station nor the junction has been studied; the geometry of the link is a study point.

Montparnasse: under a station already covered by a slab

Montparnasse has 28 platform tracks, 24 in the main station and 4 at its Vaugirard annexe.4 The platforms are one level above the street: Hall 1 is on level 2.37 They are already covered by a slab that carries a garden of 3.5 hectares, the Jardin Atlantique (unverified).38 Four metro lines meet around the station (unverified).39

The new station would have 12 platform tracks, like Gare de Lyon: 6 for TGVs, three each way, 4 for regional express trains and 2 for suburban trains. At its city end the TGV tracks fork towards Paris Nord-Est, under the Seine, and towards the direct link to Gare de Lyon, which also passes under the river. This part of Paris stands over old limestone quarries: 770 hectares of the city are undermined, in eight arrondissements that include the 14th and 15th, where the station stands.40

How deep, and why

The new platforms have to pass under what is already there: metro lines, RER stations, sewers and the foundations of buildings. At Paris Nord-Est, Magenta is already 30 m down. The model's illustration takes 35 m for all three stations assumption. That is within the range of stations that have been built, but it is not a design depth.

Depth does not strain the approaches. European rules allow tracks to slope by up to 35 mm per metre.21 A tunnel can therefore gain or lose 35 m of depth in one kilometre (derived). Platforms 35 to 40 m deep therefore need only about 1.1 to 1.2 km of tunnel to reach the surface. The portals are 2.4 to 2.9 km from the stations, on the existing tracks at the ring road (at Rosa Parks for the eastern line), which leaves room for the climb beyond the junctions; the stations are 5 to 6 km from each other through Paris Nord-Est, and the direct link between Montparnasse and Gare de Lyon is 5 km. The link does not change the argument: even at a steady 35 m, it has room to dip under the Seine and come back.

The Seine is crossed twice, once between Paris Nord-Est and Montparnasse and once on the link between Montparnasse and Gare de Lyon. Gare du Nord, Gare de l’Est and Gare de Lyon are all on the right bank; Montparnasse is on the left. Two lines already pass under the river in the centre: RER line B, on a ramp of 4%, and metro line 14 (unverified).46 36

From the hall to the coach

Deep platforms are further from the street than surface ones. But a terminal has its own long walk: the train stands beyond the gates, and the average coach is 200 m down the platform. A through station is entered from above, at several points along its length. Follow a passenger through both.

With platforms 35 m down, the deep station comes out at 4.0 minutes and the terminal at 3.7 minutes. The difference, about 18 seconds, is well inside the uncertainty of such a sketch. The figures are the same at all three stations: Gare de Lyon and Montparnasse have fewer tracks than Paris Nord-Est, which makes them narrower, not shorter, and a TGV platform is 400 m long at each. On a regional express platform of 350 m the average coach is about 44 m from a way down instead of 50 (derived). No measured times are published for the Paris terminals or for deep stations. The State's regional travel model applies a penalty to deep stations; its value is not published.48

What the model does with this

The central case takes the time inside the station as equal to today's. That is an assumption, and the result is sensitive to it: the sensitivity tests include two minutes more for every passenger, which removes 27% of the benefits.

Time inside the station is a separate matter from the time to reach its door. How long it takes to get from home or work to the entrance of a station where one's train stops is measured in reaching the station. The minutes on this page come on top, in both the present stations and the new ones.

How the station is run matters as much as how deep it is:

  • Today the platform is shown about 20 minutes before departure, and the gates close 2 minutes before.49 The passengers of a whole train, more than 1,000 when two sets are coupled, cross the hall in the same few minutes. SNCF tested showing platforms 30 minutes ahead in 2018.50
  • With fixed platforms, nobody waits for a screen. Passengers go down when they arrive and wait at the mark for their coach, as on Swiss platforms.51
  • Platforms by direction make the way down simpler. Every train for the south leaves from one of the same three platforms, so a passenger for Lyon or Marseille heads for the same part of the station every time, and the passage above the platforms needs fewer branches.
  • Two stops spread the crowd. The passengers of one train board at two stations, so each platform handles fewer people for each train.
  • The halls become waiting rooms. British design rules size a hall for the whole flow of the busiest quarter of an hour when the platform is announced late, and for a tenth of it when the platform is known in advance.47
  • London trains board differently. Their passengers pass the border checks in a control hall of their own and board from a platform closed off for the time of the stop, as described for Paris Nord-Est.

A benefit that is not counted: for trains that run every two hours or less often, the official method adds a 20-minute margin before departure.52 If fixed platforms let long-distance passengers arrive 5 minutes later, that would be worth about €223 million a year. No measurement exists of how early French passengers reach the station, so this stays out of the totals.

Chapter 4

Works, changes to today's stations, and stages

The stations would be built under four terminals that stay in use, and the tunnels under the city. This chapter shows how such works have been done elsewhere, what would change at each of today's stations, and how the project could open in two stages. The model assumes 12 years of works. That is an assumption, not a programme: there is no design and no ground investigation.

Four ways of building, all used before

Little can be dug from the street: the stations lie under working stations and the tunnels under buildings. Four methods have been used for works of this kind, in Paris or under a working terminal. Which one would serve where has not been studied.

1. A cavern dug from below

Workers reach the level of the station through a shaft, then dig the cavern from inside, a section at a time, and line it with concrete. Nothing is opened at the surface but the shafts.

  • Paris, Magenta and Haussmann-Saint-Lazare, 1999. Two stations of the RER, the express suburban lines that cross Paris underground. Each is a central vault with two side vaults, 54 m and 58 m wide for four tracks, about 30 m down.23
  • At Magenta the ground was first strengthened with 3,570 columns of injected cement, and it still gave way once during the works.23
  • The line ended 44% above its approved cost. The review names the complexity of the project and the hazards of underground work.53

2. A box built from the top down, under working tracks

Walls are sunk from the surface and a roof is cast between them. Trains run again on the roof while the station is dug out underneath.

  • Zürich, Löwenstrasse, 2014. Four tracks 16 m under the terminal tracks,8 built between September 2007 and June 2014.54 8
  • Two or three tracks at a time, normally two, were shortened by 100 m; trains ran on all the others.55 56 Part of the roof and walls had been built in advance, when the platforms above were rebuilt.57
  • Under a listed wing of the station, 110 m were dug beneath the standing building; it settled 10 to 15 mm, with 25 mm allowed.58 See the Zürich annex.
  • Paris, Porte Maillot, 2024. Where nothing stands above, the box is simply dug open: 35 m deep, in 32 months.44

3. A station under a standing building

The building is first carried on new foundations. The station is then dug underneath it.

  • Paris, La Défense, 2024. The RER E station lies under an exhibition hall. Of the hall's 253 columns, 118 were moved onto about 1,800 small piles and a slab 3 m thick.59
  • The contract ran for 61 months.60 This station was under-estimated by €100 million, one of the named causes of the 45% overrun of the extension.61

4. Tunnels bored by machine

A cutting head as wide as the tunnel is lowered down a shaft. It digs forward and lines the tunnel with concrete rings behind it.

  • Paris, RER E extension, 2024. 8 km of tunnel 30 to 40 m deep, of which about 6 km in one tube 9.6 m wide inside for two tracks, with 10 shafts for air and rescue.20
  • London, Elizabeth line. Eight machines bored 42 km of tunnel between May 2012 and May 2015.62
  • Here: 49 km of two-track tunnel, two tunnels side by side in six corridors of 2.4 to 6 km and one on the 5 km link between Montparnasse and Gare de Lyon.

Method drawings illustrative sketch, not to scale.

The link and its two junctions. The link itself, 5 km under the city and the Seine, would most likely be bored by machine, like the other tunnels. Its two junction caverns, where the link leaves the corridor from Nord-Est at the city end of each southern station, are a different matter: a cavern widening under a working station, dug from below or from the station box, with the ground and the groundwater of each site unknown. Which method they would need is not known, and the geometry of the link is a study point. Each junction cavern is carried at €250 million of works assumption.

None of these has been done at this size

The Paris caverns have four tracks and the Zürich box four; the deep through stations of Stuttgart and Berlin have eight.6 25 Paris Nord-Est would have 16, under two terminals at once, and the two southern stations 12 each. The price of that step is the largest unknown in the cost.

The project divides into two parts that can open one after the other. The costs below are with design, land and 15% risk. Whether to build in stages at all, and in this order, is a study point.

  • What it leaves. Atlantic trains still end at Montparnasse: the first stage alone gives no through train to or from the Atlantic. A passenger from Bordeaux to Lille still crosses Paris by metro, and the direct link between the two southern stations does not exist.

Whether to stop after the first stage cannot be judged yet, because its benefits on their own have not been estimated; see building in stages. The whole cost is built up in the cost chapter.

Twelve years, year by year

An assumed schedule

The model assumes 12 years of works with even spending assumption. How those years divide between tasks and stages is an illustration made for this page. It is not a construction programme: there is no design, no ground investigation and no study of how many platforms each terminal can give up while it stays open.

Move through the years to see what is being built, what is open and what passengers find at each station.

Is twelve years plausible?

Smaller projects of the same kind took seven to thirteen years, and one is past twenty. The two southern stations, with 12 tracks each, are smaller than Paris Nord-Est and may take less time; whether that shortens the critical path of the second stage is to be checked.

A longer schedule costs money as well as time, because interest runs during the works. Over 12 years it adds 20% to the cost. If the works took 15 years, the yearly cost of the project would rise by 4.0%; see the sensitivity tests.

Assumed here

  • 12 years of works, with even spending.
  • The first stage opens after year 9, the second after year 12.
  • Every terminal stays open until its deep station is ready.
  • Each park opens some years after its surface tracks close, once the tracks are cleared; the first three after the first stage, the fourth after the second.

Not known

  • The design of any station, and so the method and time needed to build it. The same for the link and its two junction caverns.
  • The ground, the groundwater and the old quarries at each site.
  • How many platforms each terminal can give up during the works.
  • Where the shafts and work sites would go, and how the spoil would leave. At Zürich, up to three trains of spoil left the site each day.56
  • How long studies, public inquiry and approvals would take before the first year.
Chapter 5

Which trains run where

The same pattern of trains is assumed every hour, and no train reverses in Paris. A high-speed train runs from the north or the east to one of the two southern stations through Paris Nord-Est, or between the two southern stations by the direct link, so each train stops at two of the three stations. In a standard busy hour, 12 trains each way run from the north or east to the south and 6 each way run between Montparnasse and Gare de Lyon by the link. That pattern, with room kept for the day the southern lines are full, sets the number of platforms.

One standard hour of high-speed trains

  • Every train stops twice in Paris, and never turns. A train from Bordeaux stops at Montparnasse, then either at Nord-Est, going on to Lille or Strasbourg, or at Gare de Lyon by the direct link, going on to Marseille. A train from Lille stops at Nord-Est, then at Gare de Lyon or at Montparnasse. Every station has direct trains to all four directions, on half of the trains of each line.
  • The same pattern every hour. The study assumes that the same trains run at the same minutes every hour. It has not drawn up a timetable, and the platform count below assumes that stops are spread through the hour. A timetable in which trains wait for each other at Nord-Est, as in Switzerland, is an option; it would need more platform tracks (see the Swiss timetable applied to Paris).
  • Platforms are fixed. The 14:07 to Lyon leaves from the same platform every day, printed in the timetable, with the place of each coach marked on the platform.51 What that changes for boarding is in the three stations.
  • High-speed trains are not for trips inside Paris. Tickets are sold from or to a station outside the region.

How many trains is a standard hour? This study takes 12 TGVs an hour each way on the Atlantic line, 12 on the south-east line, 8 on the northern line and 4 on the eastern line assumption. These are round numbers for a busy hour, not counts; the real pattern has to come from a timetable study, and what caps the number of trains today, platforms or lines, is a study point (I1 in what to verify). The second pattern below fills the two southern lines to their planned capacity: 16 trains an hour on the line to Lyon from 2030,15 and up to 15 on the Atlantic line with new signalling.4 72 No capacity figure was found for the northern and eastern lines; they are held at 8 and 4 assumption.

Any line can be paired with any other

The tunnels join all four lines, so a train arriving from one line can leave by any of the others: the northern and eastern lines meet the two southern ones at Nord-Est, and the two southern lines meet each other by the link. The timetable is free to pair them as traffic requires, and to change the pairing from one hour to the next. The choice holds at every station: from each of the three, there are direct trains in all four directions.

The four lines are not equal. The two southern lines carry more than twice the passengers of the northern and eastern ones: about 44 and 35 million a year counted at their Paris terminals, against 21.5 and 12 (derived).73 So not every train from the south can find a partner in the north or the east. In the standard hour, 4 trains from each southern line go on to the north and 2 to the east, which uses every train of the northern and eastern lines. The 6 trains left on each southern line are paired with each other by the direct link, with no reversal. When the southern lines are full, 9 an hour each way take the link and one south-east train an hour is left without a partner: it turns back at Nord-Est, the only train in the pattern that does.

For passengers, this gives direct trains on five of the six pairs of lines; only north to east has none, because the two lines meet just north of Nord-Est. Crossing Paris by TGV gives the times for each pair. Fixed pairs, with each southern line tied to one northern line, would be simpler to run but would leave only two pairs with direct trains; the model no longer tests that case, since the link makes it unnecessary.

The direct link

A train from Bordeaux stops at Montparnasse, runs 5 km under the south of Paris to Gare de Lyon, stops there and continues to Marseille. The link gives direct trains between the Atlantic and the south-east, the largest flow across Paris, in 6 minutes instead of 29 by Nord-Est with a reversal, and it keeps Nord-Est for the trains that need it.

  • What it does to the load. With the lines full, the three legs carry 6, 7 and 9 trains an hour each way. Without the link the two legs to Nord-Est would carry 15 and 16, and every Atlantic to south-east train would have to change direction at Nord-Est.
  • Length and time are assumptions. The link is taken as 5 km, within 4.5 to 6 depending on the alignment, and the 6 minutes include the stop assumption. Its geometry under the south of Paris, where old quarries lie,40 has not been designed: study point I7 in what to verify.
  • The one train that turns. With the south-east line at 16 trains an hour, one train an hour has no partner on any line. It stops at Gare de Lyon, runs to Nord-Est and turns back there, holding its platform 9 minutes, 8 to change direction with a driver at each end and 1 to clear, which counts as 2.25 stops in the platform count below. Sidings beside the high-speed depot 2 km north of Gare du Nord (unverified)63 or a run on to the airport station at Roissy are alternatives, not costed here.

How many platforms

The rule. Platforms are dedicated by direction: the tracks on one side of a station take trains heading south, those on the other side trains heading north, as at any through station. A stop takes 4 minutes; after a departure the track needs about 3 minutes before the next train can pull in; and a timetable can use about 65% of that 7-minute cycle and still absorb late trains. One track therefore takes about 5.6 trains an hour assumption, all three figures. Through stations elsewhere give the measure: Stuttgart's new station reached about six trains an hour on each track in a simulated stress test,6 7 Zürich's Löwenstrasse handles about 460 trains a day on four tracks, about six an hour on each on average,8 and Tokyo's Shinagawa was built with four tracks for 15 trains an hour each way.74 Through trains that wait for connections in Zürich stand 6 to 9 minutes (derived from the departure boards; see Zürich).9 10

Three tracks each way where two would do on paper. With the lines full, each station sees 13.1 to 16 stops an hour in each direction. Two tracks each way would take them: a train every 8 minutes on each, 4 minutes stopped and 4 empty. The third track each way takes the late trains and the trains that stand longer. The stations are sized for the day the southern lines are full. Two-minute stops, which would make two tracks comfortable, are ruled out: passengers with luggage do not board and alight a 400 m train in two minutes. Four-track stations are ruled out for the same reason, as too tight for late trains.

The sliders change the rule, not the timetable: a longer stop, a longer clearing time or a lower share of the hour used all mean fewer trains on each track.

Regional, suburban and London trains

  • Regional express trains have their own platforms, 350 m long: 6 tracks at Nord-Est and 4 at each southern station, 14 in all. The length takes three coupled Regio 2N sets, which are 81 to 135 m each (unverified). The count is the model's, not a timetable's: how many regional express trains an hour each line would run, and whether 14 platforms is the right number, is study point I3 assumption.
  • Suburban trains have 4 tracks at Nord-Est and 2 at each southern station, 225 m long, on the second pair of tunnels assumption. One imbalance needs attention: the northern and eastern lines run about twice as many trains as the southern ones (lines H, K and P 769 a weekday, lines N and R 397; about 34 an hour at the peak against 15, unverified).75 Whatever the pairing, about 19 trains an hour at the peak have no partner. Joined as here, they turn back on both southern sides, about 13 an hour beyond Montparnasse and 6 or 7 beyond Gare de Lyon, rather than all at one; some could run on as short line N trains to Versailles instead of turning assumption. The cost includes sidings for that. Whether one pair of tunnels is enough for the peak of lines H, K and P together is study point I4; a third pair of tunnels would cost about 10 billion euros more at this study's unit prices assumption.
  • London trains board from one of the six high-speed tracks at Nord-Est, closed off for each departure, with a larger control hall and waiting room above it (counted at €200 million of works assumption). At about one departure an hour and 10 to 15 minutes of boarding, that fits within the rule above. Amsterdam already boards London trains this way, from one closed-off platform.27 Trains arriving from London are checked before departure, so they can run on to the south like any other. Northbound, passengers boarding at a southern station for London would need to be checked before boarding: how, and where, is open (study point I5). Today's cross-Channel terminal at Gare du Nord is itself at its limits.26
  • Depots stay where they are; trains reach them through the tunnel portals (see changes on the surface).

Regional express and suburban trains through Paris

The second pair of tunnels joins the suburban lines two by two: lines H and K from the north run on to Montparnasse and continue as line N to the west; line P from the east runs on to Gare de Lyon and continues as line R to the south-east. The pairs also match their rhythms: the quarter-hourly branches of line H meet the quarter-hourly and half-hourly trains of line N, the half-hourly and hourly branches of line P those of line R. Regional express trains use the first pair, with the TGVs: those from the north run on to Gare de Lyon or Montparnasse, those from the east to Gare de Lyon, those from the south-east and the Atlantic to Nord-Est. What that is worth to their passengers is in regional and suburban passengers.

Chapter 6

How long to reach a station where your train stops

From the average point in Paris, a station where your TGV, the French high-speed train, stops is 27.4 minutes away today by public transport. With the three through stations it is 22.8 minutes to the entrance of the nearest station where the train stops, the measure used for the benefits of TGV passengers, or 24.5 minutes if the train’s ride between its Paris stops is counted and the passenger picks a train that calls at their best station. The stations stay where they are and the project only adds places to board, so no point in Paris is further from its train than today, for any direction.

The map: 1,000 points in Paris

Each dot is a point in Paris. Its colour shows the time by public transport from the street to a station where a TGV for the chosen direction stops. Choose a view, a way of counting and a direction, then tap a dot to read its times.

Legend

    All 1,000 points

    Tap or hover a dot to see, for each direction, where you board today and where you would board with the project.

    What “with the project” counts

    Today each direction has one terminal: Gare du Nord for the north, Gare de l’Est for the east, Gare de Lyon for the south-east, Montparnasse for the Atlantic. With the project every high-speed train stops at two of the three stations in Paris, no train changes direction, and a passenger boards at whichever stop suits best. Today’s station is always one of them. That is why the time can only get shorter.

    Trains forEvery train stops atHalf of the trains also stop at
    The north and the eastParis Nord-Est, entered from the Gare du Nord hall or from the Gare de l’Est hallGare de Lyon, for the half that come up from the south-east; Montparnasse, for the half that come up from the Atlantic
    The south-eastGare de LyonParis Nord-Est, for the half that come down from the north or the east; Montparnasse, for the half that come from the Atlantic by the direct link between the two southern stations, a ride of 6 minutes
    The AtlanticMontparnasseParis Nord-Est, for the half that come down from the north or the east; Gare de Lyon, for the half that come from the south-east by the direct link, a ride of 6 minutes

    Which trains run where is set out in how the lines are paired and the direct link. The even split between the two other stations is an assumption, and so is free entry to Paris Nord-Est from both halls. The second one matters: with entry from the Gare du Nord side only, the Paris average at the station entrance would be 23.1 minutes and not 22.8, and people who live nearer to Gare de l’Est would be further from a train for the east than today.

    There are two honest ways to count the result. The map offers both.

    To the station entrance

    22.8 minutes on average, 4.6 fewer than today.

    The minutes by public transport from a point in Paris to the entrance of the nearest station where the train stops. Where only half of the trains stop at the nearest station, the map takes the average of the two halves.

    This answers the plain question: how far am I from a station where my train stops? It is the measure used for the benefits of TGV passengers. On a trip of two or three hours, the few minutes the train then spends under Paris are spent seated on the right train with nothing more to carry or find; what matters to these passengers is a short trip to the station and no change on the way assumption. On this count 100% of the points are quicker than today, by up to 9.4 minutes.

    Counting the ride across Paris

    24.5 minutes on average, 2.9 fewer than today.

    The same, plus the train’s ride between its Paris stops when you board at the first one: 10 minutes between Nord-Est and Gare de Lyon, 11 between Nord-Est and Montparnasse, 6 between Montparnasse and Gare de Lyon by the link. The passenger picks, among the trains for their direction, one that calls at the station that suits them best, as someone who cares about time would soon learn to do, and boards at the first stop only when that still puts them ahead. It assumes enough trains an hour to choose from without a longer wait assumption, which holds on the busy lines and less so on the east.

    This answers a stricter question: how much sooner am I on my way? It is shown for TGV passengers as a test, and it is the way regional and suburban passengers are counted, for whom a few minutes matter on a short trip. On this count 99% of the points are quicker, by up to 10.2 minutes, and the rest are unchanged.

    An example. Point 275 on the map is in the 15th arrondissement, a few hundred metres from Montparnasse. Someone who lives there and travels to Lyon crosses Paris by metro to Gare de Lyon today: 29.1 minutes. With the project half of the Lyon trains come from the Atlantic, stop at Montparnasse, 4.6 minutes away, and run through the link to Gare de Lyon in 6 minutes. The other half come down from Nord-Est, and for those Gare de Lyon stays the place to board. The first measure averages the two halves at the door: 15.7 minutes. The second has the passenger always take a link train and adds the 6 minutes on the link, because until Gare de Lyon this passenger is no nearer to Lyon than someone who boards there: 10.6 minutes. The minutes on the link are spent in a seat on the right train and not in the metro, which is worth something, but they are still minutes.

    Which measure the model uses

    The time saved by TGV passengers from the Paris region, and the extra TGV journeys it brings, come from the first measure, to the station entrance. The second measure is kept as a test in the sensitivity tests. Regional express and suburban passengers are counted the other way: their gain counts the train’s ride to the station that suits them, and assumes they pick a train that goes there, in regional trains.

    The map does not include the time inside the station, from the entrance to the coach, which is a separate matter treated in boarding in a deep station; the model also tests what happens if every passenger needs two more minutes than today, in the sensitivity tests.

    How the 1,000 times were computed. A grid of 1,000 points, 315 m apart, covers Paris without its two woods. From each point the model finds the shortest time to the hall of each station on foot, by metro, RER and tram, with the average wait for each line, on the network of Île-de-France Mobilités as of 5 October 2026.76 Buses, taxis and crowding are not counted. The four directions are weighted by their share of high-speed traffic: Atlantic 39%, south-east 31%, north 19%, east 11% (derived).73 The full method is in how access times are computed.

    Who gains, and what it is worth

    Every direction gains. At the station entrance the Atlantic and the south-east gain most, because all their trains would also stop at another station, Nord-Est on the other side of the city or the other southern station through the link. Once the ride is counted, a train for Lille boarded at Gare de Lyon or Montparnasse runs under Paris in 10 or 11 minutes, quicker than the metro, and a train for Lyon boarded at Montparnasse reaches Gare de Lyon in 6. On that count the two southern directions come out best, 24.2 minutes for the south-east and 24.2 for the Atlantic against 25.1 for the north and the east, because the link gives each of them a second place to board only 6 minutes away.

    North (Lille, London, Brussels)19%27.622.84.825.12.5
    East (Reims, Strasbourg)11%27.222.84.425.12.0

    Even with the ride counted, the first stop is the better choice for a good part of Paris: for 47% of the points a train for the south-east is better boarded where it stops first, at Nord-Est or at Montparnasse, than at Gare de Lyon, and for 42% a train for the Atlantic is better boarded at Nord-Est or at Gare de Lyon than at Montparnasse. For trains to the north, 12% of the points do better at Gare de Lyon and 20% at Montparnasse, on the trains that stop there.

    The north-east of Paris gains most at the door. The 19th and 10th arrondissements (the districts of Paris) lie around and beyond Nord-Est, where every train for the north and the east, and half of the others, would stop. Today their residents cross the city for a train to Lyon or Bordeaux. Their station entrance comes 7.1 and 7.1 minutes closer on average, or 4.9 and 4.9 minutes with the ride counted. Once the ride is counted, the south-west joins them. The 15th and 14th, around Montparnasse, save 5.5 and 4.5 minutes, as much as the north-east: the link puts a train for the south-east 6 minutes from Montparnasse, where today it is a metro ride across the city. The smallest gains are in the west and the centre: in the 8th, the 17th and the 5th the entrance comes 1.8, 1.9 and 2.1 minutes closer, and little changes once the ride is counted (0.3, 0.3 and 0.7 minutes). These districts are about as far from one station as from another, so a second place to board helps them little.

    The numbers by arrondissement

    The suburbs gain a little more than Paris, because their trains and RER lines arrive on one side of the city. At the station entrance the model finds 4.6 minutes saved for a trip that starts in Paris, 5.0 in the inner suburbs and 6.5 in the outer suburbs. The map shows Paris only.

    What quicker access is worth in the model

    The model counts the whole Paris region, at the station entrance, in “equivalent minutes”: the official French method counts a minute of walking or changing as two and a minute of waiting as one and a half, because passengers dislike them more than sitting in a train.77 On that scale the average trip to the train is 5.9 minutes shorter.

    That is worth €354 million a year in time saved and brings about 2.83 million more high-speed journeys a year: British ticket data give about 11% more traffic for 10% less journey time.78 If the train’s ride across Paris were counted against the passenger, who then picks a train that calls at their best station, the trip would be 4.4 equivalent minutes shorter, worth €262 million a year and 2.09 million journeys; the model keeps that as a test, not as the central case.

    Almost all of it comes from the choice of station. With the same three stations but each train boarded only at its own, the gain would be €27 million a year. The choice between two places to board is worth €326 million a year.

    These journeys are part of the high-speed traffic forecast, and the time saved is one line of the benefits.

    Chapter 7

    Crossing Paris, by TGV and by regional train

    A passenger who crosses Paris today spends about an hour between two trains, with a metro ride in the middle. With the stations joined, five of the six pairs of lines get direct trains and none of them reverses: 6 minutes from Montparnasse to Gare de Lyon by the direct link, 10 or 11 minutes through Nord-Est for the other pairs, and a change of train happens on the platforms of one station. Suburban and regional passengers gain less on each trip, 2.7 minutes on the clock on average, but there are 116 million such journeys a year.

    TGV passengers who cross Paris

    About 107 million journeys a year by TGV, the French high-speed train, touch Paris: 102 million start or end there and 5.2 million cross it, changing between two Paris stations, usually by metro or by RER, the express suburban lines that cross Paris underground. Those who cross are counted at two stations, which is why the four terminals count 112.5 million passengers. The 5.2 million is derived from the last survey, in 2012-13: 13,000 a day in the region, 88% of them in the stations inside Paris, all kinds of train together, scaled by the growth of high-speed traffic since.2 No newer count is published, and none by pair of stations. The shares below assume that pairs follow the traffic of each station assumption. A fresh count, from the operators' ticket data, is study point I12 in what to verify.

    Atlantic and north21%57.5 min11 min23.5 min

A direct train does not suit every trip, so the estimate assumes that 50% of the passengers on those pairs find one for their own journey assumption. That makes 47% of all passengers who cross Paris; the others change inside one station, Nord-Est for most pairs.
    • North to east has no direct train. The two lines meet just north of the station, and the plan sends every train of these two lines on to the south. This is the smallest of the six flows. Passengers change on the platforms instead of walking between two stations.
    • What it is worth. €574 million a year in time saved, counted the official way, which weighs a minute spent changing as two minutes on a train.77 If every passenger on a served pair found a direct train the project would add 12.9 million journeys a year across Paris; if none did, 8.6 million. The central estimate is 10.7 million: see how many more passengers.
    • What is not known. The number of passengers itself. Counting all 13,000 of the survey, on more days of the year, gives 7.3 million instead of 5.2 million. Ticket data held by the operators would settle it (study point I12).
    • London, Brussels, Amsterdam and Cologne. Trains from London are checked before departure, so they can run on to the south like any other, and so can the trains from Belgium, the Netherlands and Germany. Northbound, a passenger boarding at Gare de Lyon for London would need a check before boarding; how that is done is open (study point I5, see how many platforms).

    The market the count misses

    The survey counts people who already cross Paris by train. It does not count those who go by car or by air between the regions because of the change of station, nor those who take the trains that go round Paris on the bypass line, with stops at Marne-la-Vallée, Roissy and Massy: 21.9 million passengers in 2009, 17.6 million of them on trains through those outer stations.16 The example below shows why many of them would rather go through: for the pairs that include the Atlantic line, the trains round Paris are slow and few. Measuring that wider market is study point I13.

    Today, with a change in Paris4h21Montparnasse to Gare du Nord by metro or RER, with the margin for the next train17
    Through Paris, with the projectabout 3h25This study's arithmetic from the best trains today: 2h04 Bordeaux to Paris, 1h02 Paris to Lille, about 20 minutes across Paris including the two stops; to verify assumption

    Regional and suburban passengers

    Suburban lines H, K, P, N and R and the regional express trains end at the four terminals today, unlike the RER. Run through, each train stops at a second station, and passengers stay on board when that station is nearer to where they are going. Suburban passengers pay nothing more for it: the Navigo pass and the Île-de-France ticket already cover the metro ride they no longer make.

    Lines H and K from the north run on to Montparnasse and join line N. Line P from the east runs on to Gare de Lyon and joins line R. The pairing follows the passengers rather than the map: line H, the busiest, gains most from the left bank, its passengers reach the job centres of Versailles and Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines without changing, and the trains left without a partner on the other side are shared between the two southern stations instead of all turning at Gare de Lyon assumption. 38.0 million suburban passengers a year would use the second station (derived from the access model: 72% of line H passengers, 19% of line R). Regional express trains do the same: those from the north continue to Gare de Lyon or Montparnasse, and a passenger takes the one that goes to the station that suits them assumption; those from the east continue to Gare de Lyon, with trains of the same type as those of Burgundy; those from the south continue to Nord-Est. 22.6 million of their passengers a year would get off at the second station, and 2.8 million would cross Paris without leaving the train, taken as 5% of today's passengers plus the gain from the change removed assumption; a count of them is study point I15.

    Trains are assumed to take 6 to 7 minutes between two stations assumption. The saving for each passenger is the difference between the trip from the old terminal to their destination in Paris and the trip from whichever of the two stops is nearer, measured on the public transport network as in reaching the station.

    The numbers as a table

    Million journeys a year. The total saves 2.7 minutes on average.

    116 million journeys a year save 2.7 minutes on the clock on average, and more with the official weights on walking and waiting, which is how the value of €161 million a year is counted.77 For line H, about half of the saving comes from being able to enter Nord-Est by either of its two halls, the rest from the second stop.

    Why two minutes matter

    • Fewer people change onto the metro and the RER at the terminals. Gare du Nord and Gare de l'Est together see 800,000 travellers a day.3 A commuter from the northern suburbs who works near Gare de Lyon no longer goes down to RER D at Gare du Nord: the train goes there.
    • Crowding counts. In a survey of Île-de-France passengers, a minute in a full metro weighed up to 1.39 times a minute in an uncrowded one when seated, and 1.55 when standing.79 The estimate carries the comfort gained at €49 million a year, in the proportion found in the appraisal of the Grand Paris Express.80 The relief of each metro line is not modelled.
    • Not counted: the relief of each crowded metro line, and more frequent trains if the lines are rebuilt as through lines. Trips from one suburb to another across Paris are now estimated, below; the region's travel model would measure them properly: study point I14. The traffic these lines could gain is in how many more passengers.

    From one suburb to another, without the metro

    A passenger from Sarcelles who works in Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines changes twice today: off line H at Gare du Nord, onto metro line 4, off again at Montparnasse, onto line N. With lines H and N joined, the same passenger stays on the train. A passenger from Sarcelles bound for Melun changes once, on the platforms of Nord-Est, from one suburban train to another going the same way.

    Each change costs passengers. British ticket data show that a journey with one more change of train loses 37% of its passengers;78 a trip that needs two changes keeps 40% of those it would have with none. The estimate removes both changes for the pairs of lines joined by a direct train, and one and a half for the others, a change across one platform counting as half a change assumption.

    How many such trips are made today is not counted by line. The 2012-13 station survey found that 14% of the trips through the Paris stations, 145,000 a weekday, run between two suburban départements and only pass through Paris.2 The estimate takes 20% of them, on lines H, K, P, N and R, as bound for a suburban line on the other side of the triangle, and shares them between the six pairs of lines in proportion to the residents along one line and the jobs along the other, fewer as the trip gets longer assumption.

The count is cautious: it keeps only the suburban lines that run through, and only trips that already pass through a Paris station. Half as many trips would bring the benefits to 70% of the cost instead of 72%; half as many again, 73%. The direct pairs were chosen for this: joined the other way, lines H and R, P and N, the same trips would be worth less, because the busiest residential line would run to the smallest job centre.

    Chapter 8

    What it would cost to build

    No design exists yet, so the cost is built from quantities (kilometres of tunnel, metres of platform) and from what stations and tunnels have cost once built. The triangle comes to about €40 billion, between €27 billion and €60 billion with low and high prices. The three deep stations are the largest item; the tunnels are close behind.

The 5 km is an estimate from the map, 4.5 to 6 km assumption.

    Why 15%

    The usual allowance for a study estimate is about 30%, and that is what this estimate carried at first. It is now 15%, for three reasons.

    • The unit prices are final costs or signed contracts, not early estimates. The first RER E figure is the final cost of the line, which includes its 44% overrun.53 The RER E stations of 2024 are the contracts of 2016 to 2018.20 59 Zürich is a final cost;81 London is the cost of the station contracts as forecast near the end of the works.82 The Grand Paris figures are contracts and the files revised in 2017.80 83 84 A price that already holds an overrun needs a smaller margin than a price taken from a study.
    • The earlier figure counted some things twice. The station price was first grossed up by 1.27, then by 1.30, for design, land and risk, before 30% was added again on everything. For the stations that counted design and land partly twice. The price is now the all-in figure from Paris, and the add-ons are applied once.
    • The back-test says where the prices sit. Before risk, they come out 28% above the first RER E section and 39% above Zürich, but 20% to 34% below the RER E extension and far below Munich (see does the method hold).

    What the 15% still covers: stations deeper than any built in Paris, under terminals that stay open throughout; and the items for which no project publishes a price (junction caverns, portals, the conversion of the halls), 16% of the works. Two study points remain: a check, item by item, of which published prices are all-in (I9), and a risk allowance set item by item instead of one rate on everything (I10).

    The prices used, and where they come from

    1. Quantities come from the layout: 49 km of two-track tunnel and 13,900 m of platform track. Platforms are 400 m for TGVs, 350 m for regional express trains and 225 m for suburban trains. The regional express length holds three coupled Regio 2N sets, which are 81 to 135 m long each (unverified).22
    2. Unit prices come from built projects, brought to 2026 euros with the French public-works index.85 That index follows contractors' costs. Prices for underground work around Paris have risen faster: the Grand Paris Express by about 15 points more between 2012 and 2020 (derived).84 Older projects are therefore understated.
    3. Design and client costs add 20%, the SNCF convention at this stage (12% and 8%).86 Land bought adds 7%; 5% to 10% is usual.87
    4. Risk adds 15% on top, for the reasons given above. The Grand Paris Express carries 24% to 32% since 2017 on prices that were estimates.84 The RER E extension carried 6% and ended 45% over budget.61

    Why €1.0 million per metre. The evidence from Paris points two ways. The first RER E stations, Saint-Lazare and Magenta, have four tracks each in caverns 30 m down, like the ones needed here. The whole 1999 line cost €2.5 billion in today's money, final; with its 4 km of tunnel deducted at our price, the stations come to about €0.9 million per metre, everything included (derived).53 The two-track stations opened in 2024 cost €0.9 million to €1.4 million per metre for their structure alone, before fit-out.20 59 The price used sits between them: it leans high against the one complete Paris figure and low against London. With design, client costs, land and risk, a metre of platform track is carried at €1.46 million, so one 400 m TGV track at about €0.58 billion all-in.

    Not priced separately: the caverns at each end of a station where two tracks fan out into many. They are taken as covered by the station price, as in a French study of a four-track deep station whose box is 938 m long for 365 m of platform.43 For a station of 16 tracks this is untested.

    Try other prices

    Move the prices within what built projects show, and the risk with them. The total and the yearly repayment follow. The repayment is what the capital account has to find each year.

    Result

    The number of TGV tracks per station can be moved too. Four-track TGV stations were ruled out as too tight for the timetable (see how many platforms); the slider shows what they would save, not that they would work.

    Does the method hold?

    The same prices were applied to seven projects that have been built or priced, and compared with their published cost.

    • Paris, first RER E section, built. The prices overshoot: €3.2 billion before risk, €3.7 billion with it, against a final cost of €2.5 billion that already includes a 44% overrun. The index used to bring 2003 money to 2026 is a floor, so the gap is smaller than it looks.
    • Paris, RER E extension, built. The prices undershoot: €4.6 billion before risk against €5.8 to €7.1 billion, depending on the price base of the published figure. With 15% risk, €5.3 billion, still 8% below the low reading. This is the project most like the one proposed, and the one the prices miss on the low side.
    • Lyon and Marseille, study estimates. Before risk the prices straddle what SNCF Réseau estimates for a deep four-track station with its tunnels: €3.5 billion against €3.8 billion for Lyon, €3.9 billion against €3.4 billion for Marseille, a figure that covers a whole phase of works. With risk, both are above the estimates, as a built cost tends to be: those estimates carry a contingency of their own, and in Paris such estimates have run 45% over.
    • Stuttgart, building. With 15% risk the prices land on the current forecast (€14.5 billion against €14.5 billion), which is in money of each year and would be higher in 2026 euros.
    • Zürich, built. The prices overshoot a final cost: €3.8 billion before risk against €2.8 billion. Zürich built a four-track station only 16 m down, under a working terminal, for half the Paris price per metre.
    • Munich, building. The prices give less than half the forecast (€4.8 billion with risk against €10.9 billion, which includes future inflation). Three stations 40 m under the centre are what a Paris project would look like if everything went wrong.
    The reading

    The prices are those of built projects, and the 15% is what separates the record's middle from its cheapest cases. It is not a cushion for an early estimate, because the prices already hold the overruns of the projects they come from. The spread between Zürich and Munich is the real uncertainty, and the RER E extension, the closest precedent, sits on the high side of the prices.

    The cost per year

    To compare a cost paid once with money and benefits that come every year, the construction cost is turned into a yearly repayment, like a loan repaid over 60 years at 3% above inflation. Money is spent for years before the first train runs: over 12 years of even spending assumption, interest during the works adds 20%. Each €1 billion of construction then costs €43 million a year.

    Running the tunnels and stations. Two French records exist. The first RER E section cost €21.3 million a year in 2003 to maintain and operate, for two deep stations and 4 km of tunnel; maintenance of the structures alone was six times the forecast.53 Brought to today with the public-works index, that is €13,200 a year per metre of platform track and about €3.5 million per km of tunnel. The RER network run by RATP costs more than €0.5 million per km of track to maintain, about €1.0 million per km of two-track tunnel.92 Stations are taken at the first figure and tunnels midway between the two, €2.25 million per km assumption. That gives €293 million a year, between €177 million and €354 million across the two records. What that does to the accounts is in the operations account.

    The State borrows long-term at 5.4% in October 2026, inflation included.93 The saving from closing the surface platforms and tracks is not deducted, because it has not been measured (study point I11). Running high-speed trains is left to their operators.

    Chapter 9

    How many more passengers

    The project would add about 13.6 million journeys a year on the TGV, the French high-speed train, and 24 million on suburban and regional trains. Most of the high-speed gain is between cities on two different lines: crossing Paris takes two or three changes of vehicle today, each of which turns passengers away, and a through train or a single change inside one station gives most of them back. The passenger charge falls only on these new uses, so no journey is lost against today: with it, 12.1 million high-speed journeys a year are added.

    What other cities saw

    Many cities have joined suburban lines through their centre and counted the passengers afterwards. For long-distance trains the record is thin: no railway has published its passengers before and after a terminal became a through station.

    • The best cases gained 24% to 30% within one to three years. Stockholm's commuter trains gained 26% in two years while the rest of the network gained 3%.102 Zürich gained 24% in the first year of its 1990 through station, with twice the trains.103 Tokyo's Fukutoshin line gained 30% in six months.101
    • Others gained little. Line E of the Paris RER, the express suburban lines that cross Paris underground, has gained about 10% so far on 30% more service.106 St. Gallen ran 25% more trains for 5% more travel.107 Philadelphia joined its two networks in 1984 during a collapse of service and saw no gain for ten years (unverified).108
    • Where a whole new line came with it, traffic multiplied, mostly by moving passengers. London's Elizabeth line joined two suburban services through a new tunnel: 56 million journeys on the two in 2019/20, 220 million in 2023/24 and 242 million in 2025/26.109 110 What made it different from a joined pair of terminal lines: new stations in the centre of the city, where the demand is, and far more trains, 24 an hour through the core. Only 9% to 10% of its journeys are new to public transport;111 in Sydney the figure is 27%.112 The annex on the Elizabeth line has the detail.

    Reading. A second stop in the city draws a real share of passengers, and removing a change of station is worth far more than the minutes it saves. But no case isolates the effect of a through station on long-distance traffic. That is why this study leans on British ticket data on changes, and on a model of time saved.
