    Suburban and regional trains: 15% more on the joined lines

    Used here: 15% more journeys on the five suburban lines assumption. The eight cases above average 16%, before deducting growth that would have come anyway. The 15% rests on the cases where lines were joined with little extra service, which is what this estimate assumes for Paris: the same trains, run through. On 136 million journeys a year that is 22 million more. The low and high cases take 5% and 25%: 8.2 and 35.3 million. Rebuilding the lines as through lines, with more frequent trains and a timetable across the region, is what gave the best cases their 24% to 30%; whether Paris would do that, and what it would bring, is study point I14 in what to verify.

    • Regional express trains. No case exists for trains whose trips are long. The time model is used instead: traffic rises about 11% when the whole journey gets 10% shorter.78 A second stop saves 2.4 to 5.4 weighted minutes on a trip taken as 100 minutes door to door assumption, which gives 5.0%, or 2.0 million journeys on 41 million. Of today's passengers, 22.6 million a year would get off at the second station and 2.8 million would cross Paris on the train, taken as 5% of today's users plus the gain from the change removed assumption (study point I15; see regional and suburban passengers).
    • A new journey is not always a new customer. Most of the growth seen elsewhere came from people who already used public transport. The financing chapter takes 30% of the extra suburban journeys as made by new holders of a Navigo pass, the travel pass of the region assumption: €15 million a year. New regional express passengers bring €16 million in fares. Together that is €32 million a year, a small sum (see more Navigo pass holders).
    • New lines take years to fill. Paris's RER D opened at 58% of its forecast and was at 84% eight years later; RER E opened at 53%.53 The figures here are for a mature service.

    High-speed trains: two gains, both counted cautiously

    Two groups of TGV passengers gain from the project, and each is estimated in its own way.

    Starting or ending in the Paris region

    102 million journeys a year today. With two stops in Paris for every train, the station where the train stops is nearer for most travellers: 5.9 minutes nearer on average, with walking and waiting counted at their official weights, to the station entrance (see reaching the station).

    The time model turns that into traffic: about 11% more for a journey 10% shorter.78 Result: 2.8 million more journeys, a gain of 2.8%. If the train’s ride between the two Paris stops were counted against the passenger, who then picks the train that calls at their best station, the saving would be 4.4 minutes and the gain 2.1 million; the central case does not count the ride, which a passenger on a long trip spends seated on the right train.

    Crossing Paris

    5.2 million journeys a year today (derived from the 2012-13 station survey, the last count made; a fresh one is study point I12, see crossing Paris). Each of them changes vehicle two or three times in Paris, from the TGV to the metro or the RER, sometimes from one metro line to another, then to the next TGV; only between Gare du Nord and Gare de l'Est is it a single change, on foot. With the project 47% of them stay on one train and the others change once, on the platforms of one station.

    Result: 10.7 million more journeys, 207% more than today, before the charge. Trains from London, Brussels, Amsterdam and Cologne can run on to the south like any other, since their passengers are checked before departure; northbound checks are open (study point I5).

    How the changes are counted. Each change of vehicle turns away part of the passengers who would otherwise make the trip: British ticket data find that an added change of train loses 37% of them in the long run.78 This study applies that loss to each change of a Paris crossing today assumption, so that a trip with two changes keeps 40% of its potential traffic and a trip with three, such as Gare de Lyon to Montparnasse by metro lines 1 and 4, keeps 25%. The number of changes for each pair of stations is read from the metro and RER map, by the route with the fewest assumption. A direct train gives the whole potential back. A passenger who still changes does so between two trains inside one station. Trains are not timed to meet, as in the Swiss pulse: each direction's trains are spaced evenly over the hour, so the wait for the next one is short. Such a change is counted as half a change assumption, the rule used here for suburban trips across Paris, and keeps 79% of the passengers. If it cost only what SBB, the Swiss railway, plans for a timed change, 12% less than a direct train,123 the gain would be 11.6 million journeys; if it cost a full change, 9.3 million. The shorter trip adds the time model on top: about 11% more travel for a trip 10% shorter, door to door.78

    What tempers it. The British loss was measured for one change of train inside a station, on routes of about 100 miles; applying it to every change of a Paris crossing is this study's reading, not a measurement. The one measurement made in Paris points lower: when the bypass line removed the change of station for trains between regions, their services carried 57% more than they would have without it (derived), new stations included.113 The low case therefore keeps the first estimate of this study, 37% on direct trains and the time model for the others: 1.6 million journeys. The high case puts every passenger of a served pair on a direct train: 12.9 million.

    The market the survey does not see. The 5.2 million are people who already cross Paris by train. The bypass line shows a wider market: its trains round Paris carried 21.9 million passengers in 2009, up from 10.2 million in 1999,16 and they are slow for the pairs that include the Atlantic line, 4h47 from Bordeaux to Lille against 4h21 with a change in Paris17 and about 3h25 through Paris by this study's arithmetic (to verify) assumption. Passengers who go by car or by air to avoid the change are not counted either. None of this is in the estimate, which applies the growth only to people who cross Paris by train today: study point I13.

    Destination by destination: time saved and traffic between cities

    Three main destinations are taken on each line: Lille, Brussels and London to the north; Strasbourg, Metz and Reims to the east; Lyon, Marseille and Montpellier to the south-east; Bordeaux, Nantes and Rennes on the Atlantic line. Their times from Paris are those of the fastest regular train (published timetables, unverified). Between two cities on different lines the trip today is the two train times plus 57.5 minutes from train to train in Paris (30 between Gare du Nord and Gare de l'Est). With the project it is the two train times plus the ride between the two Paris stops, 6 to 11 minutes, or plus a change of 12.5 minutes inside one station for those who change.

    The 54 pairs of cities: minutes today and with the project, and the growth of traffic
    • The changes matter more than the minutes. On a typical pair the trip gets 15% shorter, which alone would bring about 16% more travel. Removing two changes multiplies it by 2.5.
    • Atlantic to south-east gains most, because there is no metro line between Montparnasse and Gare de Lyon and the crossing takes three changes today; the direct link removes all three. It is also the largest flow, 35% of the passengers who cross Paris (from the traffic of each station assumption).
    • Some pairs already have trains round Paris. Lille to Lyon or Marseille run on the bypass line, with stops at Roissy and Marne-la-Vallée, and are about as quick as a through train. The growth here is applied only to people who change in Paris today, so those passengers are not counted again; whether some of them would move to the through trains is study point I13.

    Growth and supply: the estimate has none

    • The Atlantic line is short of seats. A new operator, Velvet, has ordered 12 trains to run between Paris and Bordeaux, Nantes, Rennes and Angers from 2028, and says it will add 10 million seats a year; by its own account 15% of would-be rail passengers go by car, coach or air for want of trains.18 The line to Lyon is being upgraded from 13 to 16 trains an hour each way by 2030.15
    • The central case holds traffic at today's level for the whole life of the project. The growth case lets it rise 1.5% a year: 127 million Paris-region TGV journeys a year instead of 104 million, 16.6 million added by the project instead of 13.6, and benefits worth 99% of the yearly cost instead of 70% (see the economic return). Traffic growth is study point I17.

    Capacity: what through platforms allow

    A terminal platform holds a train for 30 to 40 minutes while it is emptied, cleaned and refilled, once the margin kept behind it is counted (derived from a 20-minute planning figure and a 26-minute quickest turn-round);11 12 a through platform holds it for 4. Gare du Nord was turned down as the terminal of the airport express for lack of capacity.13 The new stations are sized for 29% more trains from the south than the standard hour assumed in this study (see how many platforms), and each of the six platform tracks at a station is loaded at 5.3 trains an hour at most against the 5.6 the rule allows. Whether the platforms or the lines outside Paris cap the number of trains today is study point I1.

    If the platforms are the cap, each 10% of extra high-speed traffic would be 11 million journeys a year, about 1 times the gain counted in this chapter, and about €191 million a year of track charges for the railway. Whether it comes depends on the lines outside Paris and on demand, so it stays out of the central case; the sensitivity test with 10% more traffic is in what could change the answer.

    More journeys, and a charge that only new uses pay

    107millionhigh-speed journeys a year touch Paris102 million start or end there and 5.2 million cross it. Those who cross are counted at two stations, hence 112.5 million passengers counted at the four terminals (derived for 2024)73
    +12.6%high-speed journeys13.6 million more before any charge, 10.7 million of them across Paris

    About 107 million high-speed journeys a year touch Paris. The project changes how they begin, end or cross the city. For the 102 million that begin or end there, a station is a little nearer and few new journeys follow: 2.8 million. For the 5.2 million that cross it, two or three changes of vehicle disappear, and traffic between the cities of two lines grows 3.1 times: 10.7 million more journeys, 1.6 million in the low case that keeps the first estimate of this study.

    The financing of the project asks something only of those who use what it adds. The passenger charge tested there is €2.55 for boarding or leaving at a station the passenger's line did not serve before, and €5.10 for crossing Paris, on a direct train or with a change inside one station. Each line still stops at its own station at today's price, so a passenger from the Paris region pays only by choosing the other station, when it saves more time than the charge is worth: 38% of them would. A passenger who crosses Paris pays €5.10 against a gain worth about €54. Nobody pays more for the journey they make today, so no journey is lost; the charge only holds back part of the gain, 1.5 million journeys a year, which is why 12.1 million remain.

    What this means

    New high-speed traffic comes mostly from the cities that Paris now separates. It adds to the case without replacing its base: the time saved by people who already travel, worth about €928 million a year to high-speed passengers and €177 million to suburban and regional ones, the parks that replace the surface tracks and, outside this estimate, room for more trains later. The crossing estimate is also the least certain figure of this chapter: the economic return adds the benefits up, and what could change the answer tests each assumption, including the low case.

    Chapter 10

    Paying to run it, paying to build it

    The money is kept in two accounts. Running the tunnels and stations would cost about €393 million a year. A charge of €2.55 on high-speed passengers who use a station their line did not serve before, €5.10 on those who cross Paris, a like charge on regional express passengers, the track charges on the new journeys and the other income found here cover 190% of it, and between 165% and 269% across what running costs could turn out to be. Repaying construction costs €1.75 billion a year; the surplus of operations pays €0.35 billion of it, and the rest has to come from taxes and grants, as for most comparable tunnels.

    Two accounts

    Two words first: TGV is the French high-speed train, and RER the express suburban lines that cross Paris underground. An operations account holds what it costs each year to keep the tunnels and stations open, and what the project earns each year. A capital account holds the repayment of construction, spread over 60 years like a loan, and the taxes and grants assigned to it. Keeping them apart answers two different questions: can the project pay its own way once built, and who pays to build it.

    The hope behind this split was that operations would pay for themselves and that the added economic activity would repay construction. The first holds, with room to spare: income covers 190% of running costs, 135% with no charge on any passenger, because the cities that Paris now separates bring 10.2 million new journeys a year across it and their track charges reach the project assumption. The surplus, €353 million a year, goes to the capital account. The second does not hold on the figures of this study: the benefits counted for the country are worth 86% of the yearly repayment of construction (see the economic return). The calculator shows what would have to change.

    The running cost is the least certain figure

    Two French records exist, and they are far apart.

    • The first RER E section (two deep stations and 4 km of tunnel, opened in 1999) cost €21.3 million a year in 2003 to maintain and operate, several times its forecast: 8.7 for maintenance of the infrastructure, 9.2 for operating the stations, 3.4 for guarding and utilities.53 Brought to today with the public-works index, that is €13,200 a year per metre of platform track and about €3.5 million per km of tunnel. The index is a choice: no official index exists for running costs, and consumer prices have risen less.
    • The RER network run by RATP costs more than €0.5 million per km of track a year to maintain, so about €1.0 million per km of two-track tunnel.92
    • Used here: stations at the RER E rate; tunnels at €2.25 million per km, midway between the two assumption. The low case takes tunnels at the RER network rate and stations at 70% of the RER E rate; the high case takes both from the RER E record.
    • Gross, not net. The new stations replace terminals whose staff, cleaning and energy are paid for today. That saving is not deducted, because it has not been measured (study point I11). It would lower the cost again.
    • The level of the charge. Operations balance without any charge: with none on any passenger, income covers 135% of running costs, 117% at the high end of running costs. The charges then pay towards construction: doubling them to €5.10 and €10.20 would raise the surplus from €353 million to €431 million a year, and hold back 2.7 million new journeys instead of 1.5.
    • The weak point is the crossing traffic. In the low traffic case, which keeps the first estimate of this study for passengers who cross Paris, income covers 99% of running costs. Most of the surplus rests on the cities of two lines travelling to each other as much as the changes removed suggest (see destination by destination).
    • What the package is worth. The regional express charge, the half share of the trainset saving and the shops together bring €122 million a year; shops at full yield would add €24 million more.
    • What to ask first. The track owner and the station operator hold the real running costs of RER E, of the stations opened in 2024 and of today's terminals. They decide whether this account balances.

    For comparison: fares cover 37% of the running of public transport in the Paris region (derived)126 and 64% in the Zürich network.127 The Elizabeth line earned £731 million in fares against £554 million of running costs in 2025 to 2026, trains included;110 it keeps its fares. Here the fares of high-speed trains belong to their operators and suburban fares to the region, which is why the project needs charges of its own.

    A charge on high-speed passengers who use what the project adds

    The proposal tested: nothing changes for a passenger who boards or leaves at the station of their own line, Gare de Lyon for the south-east, Montparnasse for the Atlantic coast, Nord-Est, entered from either historic hall, for the north and the east. Every train still stops there. A passenger who boards or leaves at another station, which their line did not serve before, pays €2.55, the price of a metro ticket in 2026.128 A passenger who crosses Paris pays €5.10, on a direct train or with a change inside one station. Each passenger can avoid the charge by doing what they do today, so the charge never makes a journey dearer than it is now.

    Who pays. A passenger from the Paris region uses the other station only when it saves more time than €2.55 is worth, about 4 minutes at the official value of time: 38% of them would, 40 million journeys a year, and they save 14 weighted minutes on average. All 15.4 million journeys across Paris pay, 8.5 million of them on a direct train.

    What it brings. €180 million a year: €101 million from the Paris region and €78 million from passengers who cross Paris.

    What it costs in traffic. No journey made today is lost, since none pays more than today. The charge only holds back part of what the project adds. In the Paris region, some passengers keep their own station when the other would save them only a few minutes, and the new journeys drawn by the time saved fall from 2.8 million to 1.9 million. Across Paris, €5.10 is 5.3% of two TGV fares; with French experts' response of traffic to fares, 0.7% fewer journeys for 1% more on the fare,129 the new journeys fall from 10.7 million to 10.2 million. With the charge, the project adds 12.1 million high-speed journeys a year instead of 13.6.

    Collecting it through the operators. The charge could also be billed to the train operators as a station charge per stop at the new stations and per train crossing Paris, rather than printed on each ticket. Operators would spread it across their fares as they see fit; passengers on the most sensitive fares would then see less of it, which is the case of a response of 0.5 rather than 0.7: 0.2 million more journeys a year. Both can be tried in the calculator.

    Is it possible in law? Two routes exist. Station charges are regulated at cost plus a return: €1,260 million a year for all French stations in 2026.130 The cost of the new stations would enter that base and be billed to train operators, who pass it on. European law also lets a track owner charge more for a specific project, on the basis of its long-term cost.131 The other route is a levy written into a budget law, as for the airport express, repaid in part by a levy on air passengers.132 133 Precedents for the level: the solidarity tax on a flight from Paris within Europe is €7.40;134 operators pay the Channel Tunnel about €35 per passenger (derived, upper bound).135 A charge that depends on the station used and on crossing Paris, not on every ticket, is a matter for the legal form chosen (study point I12). The figures here take the charge as free of VAT; if it carried the 10% VAT of tickets, the project would keep €2.32 of each €2.55.

    A charge on regional express passengers

    Regional express trains (the TER of the north, the east, the south-east and the Atlantic lines) would run through Paris on the same pair of tracks as the TGVs and call at a second station before leaving the city. The proposal tested: €2.55 for a passenger who gets off at the second station, the price of the metro ticket that passenger no longer buys;128 €5.10 for a passenger who crosses Paris without getting off. Nothing for a passenger who gets off at the first station, as today.

    Charge on regional express passengers7218% of the running cost
    • Why suburban trains carry nothing. About 38 million suburban passengers a year would also ride to the second station. Their Navigo pass or Île-de-France ticket already covers the metro ride they no longer make,128 so there is no saved fare to collect, and their gain is a few minutes, 3 to 8 depending on the line assumption. Regional express passengers from outside the region pay a separate metro fare today, and the charge replaces it.
    • No loss of traffic is modelled. The charge replaces a metro ticket at the same price, so the passenger's total fare does not rise assumption. It would be collected by the regional transport authority or the operator through the ticket, and paid to the project under an agreement.
    • Its weight. Without it, cover falls from 190% to 172%.

    More Navigo pass holders

    Navigo is the travel pass of the Paris region. Joining the suburban lines through Paris should bring new regular users: the model expects 21.7 million more suburban journeys a year (see regional traffic). A pass costs €998.80 a year whatever the number of trips,128 so a pass holder who travels more brings nothing. What counts is how many people buy a pass because of the project.

    The estimate. A regular commuter makes about 420 rail journeys a year assumption. If 30% of the new journeys are made by new pass holders assumption, that is about 15,500 passes and €15 million a year. The share is the unknown. Where it has been measured on new through lines, the share of journeys that are new to public transport was 9% to 10% in London,111 27% in Sydney (derived)112 and 28% to 32% on the East London line;136 the figure used here is at the top of that range.

    How to measure it. Count passes and validations on lines H, K, P, N and R before and after opening, and compare with lines that did not change. Passes are registered to a home address, so new holders along the joined lines can be counted directly. The regional authority's budget attributes no revenue to new lines today;126 an agreement would have to say that the measured gain is paid to the project.

    Its weight. Small either way. Fares bring the region €4.2 billion a year,126 and the project adds a few tens of millions at most. The extra running of the trains, €55 million a year, is charged to the project in the same account.

    The capital account

    Construction is paid once and repaid over 60 years. At 3% above inflation, with interest during 12 years of works, the €40.5 billion of construction costs €1.755 billion a year. Any shortfall of operations is added to it; a surplus goes to repay it. In the central case operations leave a surplus of €353 million a year.

The surplus of operations, €353 million a year, pays the rest, the same as €8.1 billion during the works. The grant alone understates the public share: it comes on top of a tax of €0.9 billion a year.
    • The business tax is a political choice, not a forecast. The existing one is committed to the Grand Paris Express until about 2071.147 It is counted here from the opening of the stations; collected during the works as well, as for the Grand Paris Express, it would bring more.

    What the country gets back

    Most of what the project returns never passes through a ticket gate: time saved by passengers of the TGV (the French high-speed train) and of regional trains, more comfortable journeys, a larger job market. Counted with the official French values, these benefits are worth €1.50 billion a year, 70% of the yearly cost of the triangle. Comparable tunnels were approved with benefits between half and twice their cost. As counted here, this project is at the low end of that range, and this chapter shows what is missing and what is still to be counted.

    Why the wider effects are small here. They are applied to the regional part only, with the Grand Paris ratio. All benefits are therefore 1.3 times the time and comfort benefits in this count, against about 2.6 for the Grand Paris Express. What can be defended for TGV links is study point I18, and the evidence points to something rather than nothing: the Cologne to Frankfurt high-speed line raised output by 8.5% in the three intermediate towns it served, an effect that halves with every 30 minutes of travel time;153 TGV links between head offices and their sites raised the margins of French groups by 0.6 to 0.8 points;154 Japanese firms found new suppliers along a new Shinkansen line.155 None of this is counted.

    Not in this count: the ticket money of train operators. The new journeys bring them about €1,079 million a year of tickets, of which the 35% paid as track charges is counted as income of the project in the operations account. What remains to the operators, once the extra trains are paid for, is not known and not counted.

    Not yet counted, and study points

    • Trainsets saved. No train waits in a terminal, so the operators need 12 to 22 fewer TGV sets, about €53 million a year at €3 million a set. Half of it is counted as income in the operations account, none of it as a benefit here.
    • Punctuality. The Grand Paris appraisal counted it; its ratio would give about €42 million a year here (derived from that appraisal). It is left out because joined lines also share their delays (see the last row below).
    • London trains running on to the south. Arrivals from London are checked before departure and could run through; roughly €43 million a year assumption, see study point I5.
    • Passengers of the bypass line moving to through trains. Province to province passengers who go round Paris today would gain about an hour through it; roughly €105 million a year assumption, study point I13.
    • Growth. Benefits are held flat. At 1.5% a year they are worth 1.41 times more over 60 years and cover 99% of the yearly cost assumption, study point I17.
    • The parks. Four park areas on the terminal sites, not valued (I19, see below).

    What public budgets get back

    Added activity pays taxes, and part of the public money spent returns to public budgets. This can be estimated, in three layers that must be kept apart because they do not have the same standing. The answer depends above all on one question that this study cannot settle: how much of the activity added around the stations is new for the country, and how much is moved from elsewhere.

    € million a year, once openNothing is newAs the appraisal counts itEvery job is new

    • Layer 1: money that reaches the Treasury because of the project. Tickets carry 10% VAT, which businesses cannot recover.156 It applies to the ticket money of the new journeys: €101 million a year in the central case. The charges themselves are taken as free of VAT. VAT lost on what passengers stop buying elsewhere is not deducted. Experience elsewhere is that this layer can be negative: the evaluation of High Speed 1 found a loss of tax of over £0.8 billion, because rail travel is taxed less than what it replaces.150
    • Layer 2: tax on added activity. France takes 43.6% of its output in taxes and social contributions.157 The rate is not in doubt; what is in doubt is how much of a local gain is new for the country. British guidance starts from the assumption that none is, unless the project is shown to bring more people into work.158 159 That is the first column. The middle column takes the wider effects as the appraisal of the Grand Paris Express counts them: each extra job is valued there at €10,000 a year of unemployment benefits saved,80 which is itself a public saving; output from denser job markets and from working time saved (for the 30% of TGV passengers who travel for work, unverified160) is taxed at 43.6%. The last column supposes that the 19,500 jobs implied are all new and each pays tax on the average output of a job in the region, €123,220.161
    • Layer 3: tax returned by the works. A simulation by the French economic observatory finds that 40% to 60% of debt-financed public investment returns to public budgets within five years, through wages, profits and lower benefits.162 This is real cash for the Treasury while the works last. It is not a gain from this project: any spending of the same size would return the same.
    How official appraisal treats taxes

    The French method does not count taxes as a benefit. It counts each euro of public money at €1.20, because raising taxes has a cost of its own, and it leaves out jobs created by the works and multiplier effects to avoid counting twice.163 The builder of the Grand Paris Express claimed up to €4 billion of tax a year for output of €10 billion to €20 billion; the State's reviewers did not endorse a tax line.164 80 For Crossrail, consultants put tax at 27% to 29% of added output.165 The table above is therefore a view for public finances, beside the appraisal and not inside it.

    The reading. Between nothing and about €1,290 million a year comes back, €440 million on the middle reading: 25% of the yearly repayment of construction, 74% on the most generous reading. Tax receipts lower the net cost for public budgets; on no reading do they repay construction.

    Against comparable projects

    The measure used everywhere is the ratio of benefits to costs over the life of the project, both brought to today's value. Above 1, the country gets back more than it spends. The ratios below are not strictly comparable, and the differences cut both ways:

    • This project is worked out over 60 years at a discount rate of 3%, with benefits held flat in the central case and growing 1.5% a year assumption in the case shown beside it, no value left at the end, running costs added to the cost, and no extra weight on public money. All benefits cover 70% of the yearly cost flat and 99% with growth; time and comfort alone 52% and 74%.
    • French appraisals (Grand Paris Express, Marseille) use 4.5%, count effects to 2140 and weigh public money at 1.2. At 4.5% over 60 years this project's ratio on all benefits falls to 0.51 flat and 0.68 with growth.
    • British appraisals deduct ticket revenue from the cost, which raises the ratio. On that basis this project stands at 1.07 flat and 1.70 with growth, against 0.70 and 0.99 on gross cost. The Elizabeth line's 1.97 becomes about 0.8 to 1.2 on gross cost, derived from its published present values: capital £9.4 billion, running £3.9 billion, revenue £7.4 billion, user benefits £11.0 billion to £15.5 billion, pounds of 2002.166
    • Australian appraisals use a 7% rate, which lowers theirs.167

    What the comparison says

    • On transport benefits alone, cross-city tunnels rarely return much more than their cost. Published ratios at approval run from about 0.5 to 2. Five of the thirteen stand below 1 on those benefits; they were built or are promoted for capacity, or rest on wider effects: Stockholm, Malmö, Gothenburg, Lucerne, the Grand Paris Express.
    • Wider effects decide the largest projects. They are a fifth to a third of the benefits in London, Sydney and Melbourne, and about 60% for the Grand Paris Express.
    • Measured returns are usually lower than forecast. High Speed 1 went from 1.5 to 0.64, Stockholm from 0.86 to 0.51, RER E from 21% to about 10%.
    • Per passenger, the cost is in the range of the others. About €178 of capital for each yearly journey, against about €150 for the Elizabeth line and about €210 for Lucerne (derived). What differs is the starting point: Paris already has five RER lines through its centre, so the project does not open a crossing that did not exist, it joins the long-distance network to it.
    • This project is below all of them as counted here, on any of the bases above. Its counted benefits are those of a mid-sized scheme. Either the count misses its main purpose, capacity for more trains and a regional network that runs through, or the project is too large for what it delivers. Telling the two apart is the first job of a study.

    What would have to be true

    Could the benefits reach the cost? Not in any case tested. The ladder below shows each favourable assumption on its own against the central case, then the cases that combine them. Each step is marked sourced when its value comes from data or built projects and assumed when it is a reasoned figure with no data behind it yet.

    Growth and capacity overlap

    Benefits can only grow 1.5% a year for 60 years if the trains can carry the passengers. The growth case therefore needs the capacity that the project is meant to unlock, and the two cannot be added to each other: the capacity line below is the condition of the growth line, not a further benefit on top of it.

    Closing the rest would take benefits that are not counted here. Three could be large enough, and each can be checked:

    1. Capacity (study point I1). If the platforms are what stops more trains from running, the project should be credited with the traffic it unlocks. For scale: each 10% of extra TGV traffic is 11 million journeys and €546 million of tickets a year, 25% of the yearly cost. Even counted in full, the gap of the central case would take about 12% more traffic, against 29% more trains planned on the southern lines. This needs the view of the track owner, SNCF Réseau, of when each terminal and each line is full, with and without the project.
    2. The regional network (I14). The count for suburban passengers rests on an average saving of 2.7 minutes and on ratios borrowed from another project. The region's travel model would show suburb to suburb trips, relief of the RER, frequency on joined lines and a real figure for wider effects.
    3. The parks (I19). About 160 hectares of tracks in the centre of Paris become four parks assumption. Their value to the city is not counted and their cost is not in the construction cost; both need a decision and a valuation.

    The tests that move the result most are in risks and next steps; the same levers can be moved by hand in the financing calculator.

    Chapter 12

    What could change the answer, and what to verify

    The case rests on a handful of things nobody has yet measured or drawn. Cost and the time needed to board in a deep station move the economic result most; the traffic that crosses Paris, more than running costs, decides how far the project pays its way once open. Most of these can be settled by studies that cost little next to the project, and twenty study points are listed at the end.

    How sure is the result?

    Each line changes one assumption and shows the share of the yearly cost that all the benefits counted then cover. The central case is 72%. These tests are run without the passenger charges, which lower the central figure by 1 point. The one test that changes only the project's income, 10% more TGV traffic once the platforms no longer cap the lines, is left out of the chart and shown in the financing chapter: more trains would bring ticket money and track charges, but the benefit of the extra journeys is not valued here, which is why the case for capacity is still to be made (see what would have to be true).

    • Cost matters most. The same benefits cover 51% to 98% of the cost depending on prices and risk.
    • Boarding time comes next. Two minutes more for every passenger removes 27% of the benefits: an extra 2.9 minutes on the clock is enough to cancel the whole gain in access. This is why the design of the Nord-Est station is the first thing to study (see inside the station).
    • How access is counted matters less. TGV passengers are counted at the station entrance. If the train’s ride between its Paris stops were counted against them, even with each passenger picking the train that calls at their best station, benefits would cover 67% of the cost assumption, study point I16.
    • Growth over time counts. Benefits are held flat in the central case. If they grow 1.5% a year, as values of time and traffic usually do, they are worth 1.41 times more over 60 years assumption, and growth needs the capacity the project is meant to unlock.
    • The money side has its own tests. Running costs, the level of the charges and the response of passengers to them are tested in the operations account and can be moved in the calculator.

    Stages and the decision

    The project can be built in two stages: first Paris Nord-Est and Gare de Lyon with the north, east and south-east corridors and the tunnel between the two stations, 26 km of twin tunnel for €26.3 billion all-in; then Montparnasse with its two corridors and the direct link to Gare de Lyon, 23 km for €14.2 billion; see works and stages. The first stage serves the trains of three of the four high-speed lines and the suburban lines of the north, the east and the south-east. Its benefits on its own have not been estimated, so this study cannot say whether stopping after it would be a better or a worse project, and the staging itself is study point I8: the order, what each stage leaves usable, and whether the link can wait.

    What to decide now

    Not whether to build. The decision today is whether to spend on seven quick tests that can confirm or stop the case:

    1. Ask for ticket data on passengers who change station in Paris, by origin and destination (study point I12).
    2. Draw one standard hour of trains with the track owner (SNCF Réseau): every TGV stopping at two of the three stations, six tracks a station, no train reversing (I2, I3).
    3. Commission a concept design of the Nord-Est station at its smaller size, 16 tracks: position, depth, time from hall to train, and a first engineer's price (I2, I9).
    4. Ask what deep stations and tunnels cost to run, from the records of RER E and of the stations opened in 2024, net of what today's terminals cost (I11). How large the surplus of operations is turns on it.
    5. Ask when each terminal and each line is full, with and without the project (I1). The economic case turns on it, and it is not valued in this study.
    6. Run the region's travel model on the two joined suburban networks: suburb to suburb trips, relief of the RER, frequency (I14).
    7. Value the parks: area, cost and worth to the city of the four terminal sites (I19).

    With those in hand, settle the level and the legal form of the passenger charges (I12, I15), fix the stages (I8), and take the case to a full appraisal.

    The case in three sentences
    • Operations pay for themselves and leave a surplus. With €2.55 on TGV passengers who use a station their line did not serve, €5.10 on those who cross Paris, the same on regional express passengers who use the second station, the track charges on new journeys and half of the operators' saving on trainsets, income covers 190% of running costs (165% to 269% across the running-cost range, 99% in the low traffic case).
    • Construction needs public money for most of its cost. The benefits counted are worth 70% of the yearly cost; a business tax package, a European grant and a grant of €11 billion add up to 80% of the €40.5 billion.
    • The judgement rests on what is not counted: capacity for the next century's trains, a regional network that runs through Paris, and four parks where the terminals stood. Those are the benefits this study could not count, and the case stands or falls on them.

    Annex A

    Zürich: a terminus that became a through station

    Zürich's main station was a terminus: 16 tracks ending at buffer stops in the middle of the city. Rather than enlarge it, the canton twice built a four-track through station underneath, in 1990 and in 2014, each with its own tunnel. The eight through tracks are under a third of the station's platform tracks and carry, on a rough count, close to half of its trains.

    Four stations in one

    Zürich Hauptbahnhof is four stations on one site: the surface hall, two underground through stations on its north and south edges, and a small terminus for two local lines under the forecourt. A level of passages and shops ties them together. The S-Bahn, named throughout, is the suburban rail network of the Zürich region. Choose a year to see the station grow, and a part to read what it is, when it opened, what it cost and which trains use it.

    Parts of the station

    The hall

    • What: 16 dead-end tracks on the surface, numbered 3 to 18, under a train shed of 1933, with seven island platforms and two side platforms.181 Track 3 is the southern edge and track 18 the northern edge.182
    • Platforms: lengthened to 420 m in 2002 to 2004.56
    • Trains: long-distance trains that end here or turn back, international trains and four S-Bahn lines.183 About 18 of the 27 long-distance departures in one hour of 2026 (derived).10
    • Before 1989: the tracks were numbered 1 to 16.181

    Passages and shops

    • What: four passages run north to south under the hall tracks. Three of them form one complex with the shops under the forecourt.183 Its two halls lie 4.7 m and 7.3 m below ground.181
    • Dates: first shops in 1970, enlarged in 1990 and 2014.181 The westernmost passage was widened from about 10 m to about 35 m in 2005 to 2008, with a lift and escalators to each platform, for CHF 56.8 million.57 184
    • Why it matters: the passages join both underground stations to each other and to the hall.8 The station's standard minimum time for a change is 7 minutes.185

    The river Sihl

    • What: the river crosses the station under the tracks in five culverts about 190 m long, each about 12 m wide and 3 m high. The bridges that carry the 16 tracks are the roof of the culverts.186
    • Under it: the roof of Löwenstrasse station lies about 1 m below the river bed,186 and its tracks 11 m below the river.57
    • During the works: two of the five culverts were dried at a time, in four stages from April 2008 to December 2010, while the river ran in the other three. The site was to be cleared and flooded if a large flood was forecast.57

    Museumstrasse station

    • What: four through tracks, 41 to 44, on two island platforms 360 m long, 13.6 m below the street of the same name on the north side.181
    • Opened: May 1989 for a few regional trains,181 and 27 May 1990 for the S-Bahn.187
    • Trains: S-Bahn only, 11 lines.183 Up to 20 trains an hour each way at the peak.103 Stadelhofen, the next station on the same lines, sees 770 trains a day.188
    • Cost: part of the line of 1990, CHF 866 million in all.189

    Tunnels to the east

    • What: the Hirschengraben tunnel, 2.1 km underground of which 1.3 km bored, leads to Stadelhofen station; the Zürichberg tunnel, 5.0 km, carries on to the suburbs.190 191 About 12 km of new line in all.103
    • Opened: 27 May 1990, after nine years of works.187
    • Cost: CHF 866 million with Museumstrasse station, of which the canton paid 80%.189
    • Today's limit: Stadelhofen has three tracks and is described as the largest bottleneck of the S-Bahn. A fourth track with second tunnel tubes is planned for 2027 to 2037 at CHF 1.1 billion.188

    SZU terminus

    • What: two dead-end tracks, 21 and 22, with one island platform 125 m long, 11.6 m below the forecourt.181 SZU is a separate local railway.
    • Opened: 5 May 1990. It uses a section built ahead for an underground railway that voters rejected in 1973.192 193
    • Cost: a credit of CHF 72.4 million, approved by 67% of voters in 1983.193
    • Trains: two local lines, to the Sihl valley and to the Uetliberg, about seven trains an hour.192

    Sihlpost wing station

    • What: four extra dead-end tracks, 51 to 54, on the surface south of track 3 and set back from the hall. In service from 2003, closed on 15 June 2014 and removed.182
    • Trains: the S-Bahn lines S1, S2, S8 and S14, which turned back here.194
    • Why: it freed hall tracks for the national timetable of 2004. The government accepted it only as an unavoidable stopgap: it met broad opposition because of longer changes and worse access to the city centre.194

    Löwenstrasse station

    • What: four through tracks, 31 to 34, on two island platforms 420 m long and 13.5 m wide, 16 m below hall tracks 4 to 9.8 56 The whole structure is 675 m long.8
    • Opened: 15 June 2014 for the S-Bahn, 13 December 2015 for long-distance trains.195 196
    • Cost: CHF 674 million for the station.81
    • Trains: 460 a day, of which 140 long-distance and 320 S-Bahn.8 In 2026: four Intercity lines between western and eastern Switzerland, one regional express and the trains to Munich.10
    • Built under the working hall: its roof and walls were laid in 2002 to 2004, when the platforms above were being rebuilt anyway.57 See the lessons.

    Weinberg tunnel

    • What: 4.8 km, two tracks in one tube more than 11 m across, from the east end of Löwenstrasse station to Oerlikon.8 It passes under the river Limmat and 5 m below the Hirschengraben tunnel, then turns through about 180 degrees to reach Oerlikon from the south.197
    • Built: main drive from June 2010, breakthrough on 22 November 2010.198 Opened with the station on 15 June 2014.195
    • Cost: CHF 498 million.81
    • Trains: 12 S-Bahn trains an hour each way at opening.195 Main station to airport in 9 minutes by Intercity.199

    Bridges to the west

    • What: two bridges, 1,156 m and 394 m long, carry the new line in from Altstetten, to the west.8 A ramp leads down to the station; the approaches slope at up to 37 mm per metre.198
    • Opened: December 2015. Long-distance trains have run through the station since then.8 196
    • The whole line: 9.6 km from Altstetten to Oerlikon.200

    Details cited to Wikipedia in these descriptions are unverified: the layout of the hall and the lines that use each part, the sizes and depths of Museumstrasse station and of the SZU terminus, the levels and dates of the passages, the lengths and route of the tunnels, the figures for Stadelhofen, the dates of the wing station and the vote of 1983.

    Why through platforms, and not a bigger terminus

    Twice the first plan was something else, and twice voters chose a through station by a large majority.

    YearWhat happened
    1973Voters reject a credit of CHF 599 million for an underground railway with an S-Bahn: 57% no.193
    1981They approve CHF 523 million for the S-Bahn alone, with a through station under the north edge of the main station: 74% yes.193 189
    1990The line opens after nine years of works.187 On a working day, S-Bahn traffic at the city boundary is 24% higher in the first year.103
    1990sFor the national timetable of 2004, the railway plans a wing station beside the hall for four S-Bahn lines, and two more tracks on the viaduct towards Oerlikon: about CHF 650 million, plus CHF 200 million to CHF 300 million further out.201 202
    1997 to 1998Residents of two city districts resist the wider viaduct, and the canton's heritage and noise offices oppose it.56 203
    1999A popular initiative, "For a through station, no wing station", asks for a tunnel and an underground through station. The government answers with a proposal of its own and the initiative is withdrawn.204
    2001Over 80% of the canton's voters (82% in the engineering press) approve CHF 580 million, the canton's 40% share of an estimate of CHF 1,450 million.184 58 204
    2003The wing station opens all the same, as a stopgap, and closes the day the through station opens in 2014.182

    The vote shares of 1973 and 1981 and the dates of the wing station are from Wikipedia and unverified; the canton confirms the date and the amount of the vote of 1981.

    The reasons given at the time were not journey times first.

    1. The terminus could not grow where it stood. The government found the scope to develop the station at its site and level "severely limited". A new main station on another site was examined and dropped.194
    2. The bottleneck was the line out, not only the platforms. Towards Oerlikon and the airport, more trains were "hardly possible". A through station joined to a new pair of tracks was called "the key element".194
    3. The wing station put passengers too far from their connections. The initiative called the walk from there to the express trains unacceptable; a through station under the hall gives "the most direct connections to the other tracks".194
    4. Turning back wastes platforms and tracks. The trade press called it "a time waster" and an "inefficient use of platform and track space".205 The canton listed the end of the reversal among the gains.206
    5. It was built for long trains from the start. The canton judged that the S-Bahn alone would never fill a second through station. Platforms of 420 m instead of 300 m cost just under CHF 30 million more.194

    The result, as stated by the engineers: four through tracks raised the capacity of the whole station by about one third.56 The gain was not published in trains per hour.

    How to read it. A through train that waits for connections still stands 6 to 9 minutes. Only a train that does not wait shows the bare stop of 3 minutes, and a train that turns back can leave after 5. So the length of the stop is set mainly by the connections, not by the reversal (derived). What the through station removes is the reversal itself, the crossing of other trains' paths on the way in and out, and several minutes of approach. Where a locomotive must be changed at a reversal, that alone takes 4.5 minutes.185

    The benchmark for Paris. The four through tracks of Löwenstrasse take about 460 trains a day,8 about 6 per track an hour on average over a service day of 19 to 20 hours (derived). The rule used for the Paris stations sizes a high-speed track at about 5.6 trains an hour: a stop of 4 minutes, 3 minutes between a departure and the next arrival, and a timetable that uses 65% of that cycle assumption. With the lines full, the six tracks provided at each station are loaded at 4.4 trains an hour per track at Nord-Est, 5.0 at Montparnasse and 5.3 at Gare de Lyon: see how many platforms. The two counts are not quite alike. Zürich mixes long-distance and suburban trains on the same four tracks, and its trains bunch around the hour; Paris gives regional express trains their own platforms and spreads the stops through the hour.

    What changed

    +1/3capacity of the whole stationFrom four more through tracks, as stated by the engineers56
    460trains a day under the hall140 long-distance and 320 S-Bahn at Löwenstrasse8
    1 in 3long-distance trains runs through9 of 27 departures and 8 of 25 arrivals in one hour of 2026 (derived)10 9
    6minsaved on the S-Bahn across the cityFrom Oerlikon through the main station to the left shore of the lake195

    Traffic. The first through station changed the S-Bahn most. On a working day, 159,288 passengers crossed the city boundary by S-Bahn in the year before it opened, 196,854 in the first year after, and 445,562 in November 2014: 180% more in 24 years, with twice as many trains an hour at the peak.103 From 2014 to 2019, with the second through station, S-Bahn traffic grew by a further 19%.104 How much of this growth is due to the stations themselves cannot be separated from the growth of the region and of the service.

    Trains. The station handled about 1,400 trains a day around 2000 and about 2,000 in 2007.212 54 Around 2020 it handled 2,915 train movements a day, of which 2,607 passenger trains (unverified).182

    Journeys. S-Bahn trains cross the city about 6 minutes faster and long-distance trains up to 7 minutes faster; the main station is 9 minutes from the airport.195 213 199 A few journeys became longer.

    Some loseThe Basel to airport train, now routed through the main station, takes about 10 minutes between Altstetten and Oerlikon instead of 6 to 7.206 Passengers of one local line wait about 15 minutes longer for long-distance trains; the government answered that perfect connections for all would cost too much.216

    Cost. The line of 1990 cost CHF 866 million in the final account. The canton paid CHF 693 million, 80% of it: CHF 14 million less than its credit of CHF 523 million once CHF 69 million of approved extra works and CHF 114 million of inflation were added.189 The cross-city line of 2014 and 2015 was put to voters at CHF 1,450 million at 2000 prices.204 Its final account is CHF 2,052 million at 2005 prices, 1% above the ceiling of CHF 2,031 million agreed in 2008; the canton paid one third and the Confederation two thirds.81 In this study's 2026 euros the line comes to about €2.75 billion.

    Punctuality: no figure is published for Zürich before and after the through stations. The regional transport authority states that the main station now has enough capacity for the growth expected in the foreseeable future and that timetable stability improved across Switzerland.8

    What Paris can take from it, and where the comparison stops

    What carries over

    • Put the through tracks where the trains already are. Both new stations lie under the old hall or right beside it, and one level of passages serves all of them. The wing station beside the hall was accepted only as a stopgap, because of the walk.
    • A few through tracks do a lot. Four of them added about a third to the capacity of the whole station.56
    • Build for long trains at once. Platforms of 420 m were a small extra cost, and they are why Intercity trains use the station today.
    • It can be built under a working station. The roof slab, walls and columns went in first, from the surface; the station was then dug out under the slab. Normally two hall tracks at a time (two to three in the engineering press) were shortened by 100 m, leaving about 300 m of platform in use, and trains kept running on all the other tracks.55 56 The listed south wing of the station building was underpinned and settled by 10 to 15 mm, against 25 mm allowed.58 For Paris, see building methods.
    • The cost held once the works were let, not before. The second project ended 1% above the ceiling agreed in 2008, but that ceiling was 40% above the estimate put to voters in 2001, in prices five years older.81 204

    Where the comparison stops

    • Size. Each Zürich through station has 4 tracks. Paris Nord-Est would have 16, of which 6 for high-speed trains, 6 for regional express trains and 4 for suburban trains; the three Paris stations together would have 40. Zürich is no evidence for a station of that size.
    • The hall stayed. About two thirds of Zürich's long-distance trains still end or turn back in the hall (derived). The Paris project moves all main-line trains underground and keeps no surface hall for trains. Zürich shows that through platforms relieve a terminus, not that they can replace one.
    • Trains and length. The platforms compare: 420 m in Zürich, 400 m for a double high-speed train in Paris.21 The traffic does not: 140 long-distance trains a day use Löwenstrasse, about nine departures an hour. The pattern tested for Paris has 12 high-speed trains an hour each way running through Nord-Est and 6 more each way on the direct link between Montparnasse and Gare de Lyon: see the hour.
    • Depth and price. Löwenstrasse lies 16 m down and was dug from above. In 2026 euros it cost about €0.55 million per metre of platform track (€0.5 to 0.6 million), and that is a final cost. This study uses €1.0 million for the deeper Paris stations, a planning price with 15% risk added on top: see the prices.
    • Stops. Running through did not shorten the stop of trains that wait for connections. A train that turns back in Zürich stands 5 to 12 minutes. In Paris no train is planned to reverse: every high-speed train calls at two of the three stations and runs on. The one exception: when the lines are full, 1 train an hour from the south-east is left without a partner and turns back at Nord-Est: see the direct link.
    • Time. Nine years from vote to opening for the first station, and fourteen for the second, from the vote of 2001 to the long-distance trains of December 2015.
    The reading

    Zürich supports three claims of this study: through tracks under a terminus add much capacity for their number, they can be built while the station works, and voters will pay for them when the alternative is a worse station further away. It does not support the size, the depth or the cost of the Paris stations, and its long-distance trains gained less time at the platform than one might expect.

    Annex B

    The Elizabeth line: joining two sides of a capital

    London's Elizabeth line is the closest recent case of joining two sides of a capital by a deep tunnel with large stations. It opened in 2022, three and a half years late and 28% over budget. It now carries more than 700,000 trips a day and its fares cover its running cost, yet most of its passengers were already on rail and save a few minutes each. It is also far smaller and simpler than what Paris would need.

    The line and its stations

    Stopping trains from the west used to end at Paddington station, and stopping trains from the east at Liverpool Street station, two terminals at the edge of the centre.217 The project, called Crossrail while it was built, joined them with 21 km of new twin tunnel under central London, one tube for each direction, and added a branch to the south-east.218 The result is one line of more than 100 km and 41 stations, 10 of them new.219 It is run by Transport for London (TfL), the city's transport authority.

    Each mined station has two platform tunnels of about 240 m, and most have a ticket hall at each end, so that one station spans two older ones.225 226 The underground stations have platform screen doors, glass walls between the platform and the track.227 All 41 stations can be used without steps.221

    Journey times before and after

    Paddington to Liverpool Street takes 11 minutes instead of about 20.224 The largest gains are on the new south-east branch, which had no direct railway to the centre. On the older branches the saving is smaller, but the change of train at the terminal disappears. Where the Underground already ran directly, the line saves nothing.

    What the official evaluation measured

    TfL and the national transport ministry published an evaluation of the first two years in 2025.223 It counts perceived minutes: minutes weighted for waiting, crowding and delay, as a passenger feels them.

    A weekday of October 2023TripsMinutes saved per tripMinutes saved in all
    New public transport trips71,0006.3447,000
    Trips already made, anywhere in London6,429,0001.38,552,000
    All trips6,500,0001.48,999,000
    • Small savings for many people. 95% of the minutes saved go to trips that were already being made (derived), including on other lines that became less crowded.
    • Measured from door to door, the typical peak journey between the Paddington area and the Abbey Wood area fell from 74.5 to 45 minutes between 2019 and 2023.223
    • Along the older branches many routes show no significant fall, since trains already ran there. The report gives no minutes for the change of train that disappeared.223
    • The size of the saving that carried London's case is 1.3 perceived minutes a trip across all trips, 6.3 for the new ones;223 this study counts about 2.7 clock minutes a journey for the regional passengers who gain a second stop in Paris, before any weighting: see regional traffic.

    How traffic grew, and where it came from

    The line opened in three steps over twelve months, and traffic rose at each one. Against the last year before the pandemic, yearly journeys have multiplied by 4.3: from 56 million on the two older services to 242 million in 2025/26 (derived).109 110

    Where the passengers came from

    • New trips are about a tenth. The evaluation finds 71,000 more public transport trips a weekday across London, about 1% of the city's total and a tenth of the line's own (derived).223 TfL's first estimate, a year after opening, was twice that (unverified).260
    • The older services kept their traffic; the growth is elsewhere. The traffic that came from them equals about 58 million journeys a year, almost what they carried in 2019/20 (derived).259 109
    • Other lines were relieved. Parallel rail links carry 16% to 22% less than comparable links (derived).223 The line itself has room: in January 2024 it was never above 3 standing passengers per square metre.223

    What multiplied the traffic, and what Paris would have of it

    Three things multiplied the journeys by 4.3. Six new stations were opened in the centre, on a route that had no railway, each spanning two older stations and joined to the Underground. Trains run through instead of ending at Paddington and Liverpool Street, so the change of train at the terminal disappeared. And there are far more trains: 24 an hour through the centre against 15 or 16 into the Liverpool Street terminal before, plus a new branch to the south-east.221 249 The three stations of this study give Paris the second of these, and part of the first: the second stop in the centre is a new station for the passenger who used it, though not on a route without rail. They do not give the third. The model keeps today's trains on the suburban lines and adds regional express trains only; it counts the time saved by the second stop and the journeys that follow from it, at 23.7 million a year, and nothing for more trains, less crowding or journeys across the region. Those are left to study point I14: see what must be verified.

    What this says for a forecast

    Most users of a new through line are people already on rail who save a few minutes. New trips are about a tenth, and the shift from cars is close to nothing. Demand rose 6% to 9% where journeys became 10% shorter.259 This study builds its regional forecast the same way, with an average saving of 2.7 minutes a journey: see regional traffic and the evidence.

    What it cost, who paid, and what came back

    In 2026 euros the final cost is about €32 billion, an order of magnitude converted for this study with British consumer prices and the exchange rate of October 2026.69 262 263 The tunnels were finished in 2015.62 The time was lost afterwards, in the stations and in making trains, signalling and station equipment work together; the delay became apparent only in late 2018.264 Of the last £1.9 billion of cost increase, £0.9 billion was the cost of the delay itself.265

    Who paid

    The supplement on business rates. Business rates are the British tax on business property, charged on the rental value of the premises. Since 2010 London adds 2 pence per pound of that value, the legal maximum, on its larger premises, 13% of them.261 The supplement was to pay £4.1 billion, 28% of the budget of 2010 (derived).242

    The overrun was covered by government loans, most of them to the Greater London Authority, the city's government.265 With a levy on new floorspace paid by developers, the Authority's contribution reached £6.9 billion, 37% of the final funding of £18.8 billion (derived).261 69 It borrowed the money and repays it from the two levies. The supplement is due to end between 2038 and 2041.261

    Fares and running cost

    The line earns more in fares than it costs to run: £177 million more in 2025/26 (derived).110 Two cautions. The surplus is about half of what the Authority pays each year on its loan, and the two sit in different accounts. And at most about half of the income is new to TfL: the rest was already paid on its other lines (derived).259

    For Paris the picture is similar, for another reason. The project keeps no fares of its own, but in the central case of this study the track charges on new high-speed journeys and the charges on new uses cover 190% of the yearly running cost with the whole income package, 165% with the charge on high-speed passengers alone and 135% with no charge at all. Most of it rests on the new traffic across Paris, the least certain figure of the study: see the operations account. How London's supplement serves as a precedent is in the financing precedents.

    Benefits against costs

    A benefit to cost ratio divides what a project is expected to bring, counted in money over 60 years, by what it costs. Above 1, it gives back more than it costs. "Wider benefits" are gains beyond time saved, mainly the extra output of firms and workers brought closer together; they are harder to estimate.

    The same ratio on two bases. British appraisals deduct the fares from the cost before dividing. The 1.97 of 2011 divides the benefits by a cost net of fares of £5.9 billion: capital 9.4, running 3.9, less revenue 7.4, present values in pounds of 2002. User benefits were put at £11.0 billion valued as the national ministry does and £15.5 billion as London does.166 This study divides by the gross cost. On that basis the Elizabeth line stands at about 0.8 with user benefits valued as the national ministry does and 1.2 as London does (derived); this project at 0.70 on gross cost and 1.07 on cost net of its income, 0.99 and 1.70 if traffic and benefits grow by 1.5% a year: see the benefits.

    What the official evaluation does not show
    • No value for money yet. "It is still too early for an in-depth analysis of the Elizabeth line's value for money."223
    • No result on property or tax. No measured effect on property values or on tax receipts has been published. The figures in circulation, such as "£42 billion added to the economy", are forecasts made by the promoter before the opening.166 165 270
    • Homes and jobs without a cause. 71,000 homes were built within 1 km of stations from 2015 to 2024, and jobs grew, mostly in the City, where the report cannot tell the line's effect apart.111

    What Paris can take from it, and where the comparison stops

    What Paris can take from it

    • The risk is in the stations and the systems, not in the tunnels. Main station contracts tripled or more: Paddington from £181 million to £571 million.82
    • Do not fix the opening date early. The project was "dominated by a fixed completion date" set eight years ahead.264 The official lesson: "Use an evidenced range rather than a single target date."272
    • Fewer contracts, and one body in charge of the joins. With 36 main contracts and nobody but the client managing the joins between them, the client paid for knock-on delays.82
    • Protect the testing period. Trains switch between three signalling systems.82 Preparing the line for service took 14 months against 4 assumed.249
    • Open in stages, and plan the stages again when delay comes.249 For Paris see the stages.
    • Price the stations with care. London's central stations cost €2.0 million per metre of platform track, twice the €1.0 million used here. At the London price the three Paris stations would cost about €20 billion more: see the prices used.

    Where the comparison stops

    • London built a large metro. One kind of train, 205 m long. Its 24 trains an hour need only two platform tracks per station. No long-distance train uses the tunnel.
    • Paris would take 400 m high-speed trains. They stand longer at the platform than a metro, so Paris Nord-Est needs 16 tracks, 6 of them for high-speed trains: see how many platforms. Nobody has built a deep station of that size.
    • London joined two suburban networks. Paris would join four high-speed lines, four regional express corridors and five suburban lines, through three stations instead of one line.
    • London had no fast line across its centre; Paris has five. The RER lines already cross Paris, so the gain for each regional passenger is a second stop, not a new railway. That is why the model counts 23.7 million new regional journeys a year on 116 million users, where London multiplied its traffic by four.
    • The cost is larger: €40 billion (€27 to 60 with low and high prices) against about €32 billion, for 2.3 times the tunnel.
    • London's fares pay for running the line. In this study the new income covers 190% of the running cost, 165% with the charge on high-speed passengers alone, most of it from the track charges on new journeys across Paris.
    • A planned frequency is not a promise. The line runs 16 trains an hour at quieter times where its sponsors required 20.252
    The reading

    The Elizabeth line shows that a through tunnel under a capital fills up fast, relieves the lines beside it and can pay for its own running. It also shows that most of the traffic is moved from other lines, and that stations and systems decide cost and delay. Its evaluators warn against carrying the results to other places.223 Zürich, the other precedent, is closer to Paris in kind, with long-distance trains under a working terminal: see Zürich main station.

    Annex C

    The Swiss pulse: every train meets every train

    In Switzerland the timetable was designed first and the works second. Trains from every direction reach the main stations just before the hour and leave just after, so that almost any change takes a few minutes. Lines were made faster only as far as needed to run from one such meeting to the next in under an hour.

    The idea: all the trains are in the station together

    A regular-interval timetable repeats itself every hour: each line leaves at the same minutes all day. The Swiss network has had one since 23 May 1982.273 The pulse adds a second rule. At the main stations, called nodes, the trains of all lines arrive at about the same time and leave again together a few minutes later.274 In the words of SBB, the Swiss federal railway, trains and buses reach a node just before the full and the half hour, or at minutes 15 and 45, and leave shortly after.275 The passenger does not hunt for a connection: it is standing at another platform.

    :45

    Arrivals

      Departures

        Minute, line, place and track for the wave around the full hour. Tracks 31 to 34 are the through platforms under the hall.

        The station's standard minimum for a change is 7 minutes.185 Shorter changes exist where the planner names the pair of trains: Bern to St. Gallen is sold with 4 minutes, because the two trains stand on the two sides of one platform.215 Where no value is set, Swiss timetable data assume 2 minutes.276

        The nodes and the minute at which they beat

        The plan of 1994 named seven nodes. Zürich, Basel, Bern and Winterthur are served at the full hour and, for a large part, at the half hour. Lausanne, Biel and Luzern are served at minutes 15 and 45, because the runs to them are slightly too long for the hour. A node at 15 and 45 needs a train every half hour to give good connections.274

        The 2026 timetable still shows Zürich, Bern and Basel at 00 and 30, and Lausanne and Biel at 15 and 45. Luzern now gathers its trains around the hour, and St. Gallen behaves as a node of its own (derived from the timetable). Choose a station or a line.

        Why a run must take just under an hour

        If every train is in Zürich at the hour and every train is in Bern at the hour, a train between the two has just under an hour for the run. The Federal Council put it in one sentence: the concept requires journey times between the nodes of a little under one hour.274 In general the run, with half the stop at each end, must fit a multiple of half the interval: 30, 60 or 90 minutes for an hourly service (unverified).293 Hence the Swiss motto of 1986: not as fast as technically possible, but as quickly as necessary.277

        The same thing on the real board. In 2026 the train from Zürich reaches Bern at :58. The trains to Basel and to Lausanne and Geneva leave at :04, the train to Visp and Brig at :07.294 279 With the 69 minutes of before 2004, it would arrive at :11, after all of them (illustration).

        Where the hour cannot be reached, the node moves. Bern to Lausanne takes 69 minutes, so Lausanne is a node at 15 and 45: the train leaves Bern at :34 and arrives at :43.297 274 Official maps show slots of 60 and 75 minutes on these western lines.298 A target of 57 minutes exists but has not been met,299 and the plan for 2035 assumes 68.300 The western cantons speak of a two-tier network.301

        What it took

        • A vote. On 6 December 1987, 57.0% of voters approved Rail 2000, on a turnout of 47.7%.302
        • A budget that was cut to fit. The credit was CHF 5.4 billion at 1985 prices, about CHF 7.4 billion at 1993 prices. By 1991 the railway's plans would have cost about CHF 16 billion. The first stage was then capped at CHF 7.4 billion.274 Of four new lines in the plan put to voters, one was kept.303
        • One new line. Between Mattstetten and Rothrist, on the way from Bern to Olten: 45 km (47 km in two official papers), for CHF 1.5 billion in the press of 2002 and CHF 1,458 million in the budget of 1994.295 304 275 274 It brought three runs to about one hour at once: Zürich to Bern, Bern to Basel and Bern to Luzern.
        • Trains instead of concrete elsewhere. On the line along the Jura from Lausanne to Zürich through Biel, tilting trains were bought instead of new line. Double-deck coaches gave 40% more seats without longer platforms.274 Works were done only at bottlenecks or where a run between nodes took more than 60 minutes.305
        • The outturn. The first stage opened on 12 December 2004 and cost CHF 5.9 billion, CHF 1.5 billion under its ceiling.304 295

        Three runs came to about one hour with the new line. Three others, in the west, are still 8 to 11 minutes over the hour, and all three are slower than planned in 1994.

        • How much is due to the pulse? The official evaluation credits slightly under half of the growth of 1996 to 2005 to the change in service. It judges the coordination of long-distance and regional trains at the nodes a success, but it could not separate the effect of the pulse from that of speed and frequency.314
